#3490. 10 Books Like ‘A Court of Thorns and Roses’ You Should Read Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Sarah J. Maas’ lush, romance-soaked series A Court of Thorns and Roses has blossomed into a sprawling, complex fantasy series with millions of dedicated fans, and with good reason. A complex heroine who keeps discovering new depths in herself, fascinating supporting characters who shift from antihero to antivillain in unexpected ways, creative and beautifully rendered world-building—the series has it all, while also being unapologetically romantic (and steamy).

The story of a huntress who is kidnapped by a fae prince and brought to the Spring Court as a prisoner, only to become a key player in all that fae drama, ACOTAR is special, but Maas can only write so fast. If you need more books with the same lush feel, here are 10 to get you started.

It’s no shock that one of Sarah J. Maas’ other series would be recommended for fans of A Court of Thorns and Roses, but there’s a specific reason you should jump into her Crescent City series, especially the third book, House of Flame and Shadow. The most recent ACOTAR book, A Court of Splintered Harmony, revealed that the events of House of Flame and Shadow tie directly into the events in Splintered Harmony, particularly with regard to the character of Feyre’s sister, Nesta. In other words, if you read Splintered Harmony and wondered why Nesta was being so weird, there’s a whole other book series you should dig into immediately.

If Feyre’s grit and determination are your favorite aspect of ACOTAR, Julie Kagawa’s Iron Fey series (starting with The Iron King) will be your next obsession. Meghan Chase has never felt ‘normal’ in her life, and she’s been haunted by her father’s disappearance since she was a child. When her brother also vanishes, she goes on a quest for answers, learns that she’s actually the daughter of a faerie king, and finds herself in a magical world that blurs in elements of Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream. Meghan is determined to save her brother (and herself), but a certain ice-cold fae prince captures her attention, even though he’s as dangerous as he is beautiful.

If you’re looking for some serious romance in your fantasy, Jennifer L. Armentrout’s A Blood and Ash series is a must. Poppy was chosen at birth to be the kingdom’s Maiden, isolated and untouched in order to be ready for her Ascension to ensure the land is protected from the evil force that took her family. But it’s a lonely existence—until Hawke is assigned as her sworn protector. Golden-eyed and beautiful, Hawke offers Poppy the connection she’s craved. When chaos erupts around her, Hawke takes the opportunity to spirit Poppy away. But Hawke has a secret, and Poppy is soon in danger of losing both her heart and the favor of the gods themselves.

If you love how A Court of Thorns and Roses takes the “enemies-to-lovers” trope and builds it into a deep, complex mesh of emotions and plot twists, you’ll love Shelby Mahurin’s Serpent & Dove series. When witch Louise le Blanc flees her coven, she takes shelter in the city of Cesarine, where magic is forbidden, and witches are unceremoniously hunted and burned. Louise’s life gets infinitely more complicated, dangerous, and steamy when she’s trapped into an unwanted marriage with Reid Diggory—who happens to be a huntsman of the Church, charged with tracking down and eliminating witches. And then Louise starts to realize that Reid is actually pretty darn hot.

If you’re looking for a romantasy that’s broadly similar to ACOTAR while being its own thing, read A.K. Mulford’s The Five Crowns of Okrith series, starting with The High Mountain Court. Remy is a red witch, which means she’s in hiding and ready to make a run for it if the fae get near. So when a group of fae shows up at her tavern, she makes for the exit—only to be captured by Prince Hale of the Eastern Court. Instead of striking her down, however, Hale asks Remy for help—he needs to locate two ancient magical artifacts created by red witches, and he needs her red magic to find them. Hale promises to set her free and even reunite her with the red witches still living. More importantly, Remy finds Hale irresistible and has a primal urge to stay with him, no matter what the cost.

Looking for a romantasy with a slightly different vibe from ACOTAR? Variety is the spice of life, after all—and The Fourth Wing delivers. Rebecca Yarros’ Empyrean Series made a huge splash when it debuted, and for good reason—it has everything, from a capable, intelligent heroine thrust into a dangerous scenario (in this case, a dragon rider academy where failure can be deadly) and forced to navigate alliances, conspiracies, and her own heart, which is pushing her towards a romance that might be as dangerous as the dragons themselves.

Love the moral complexity of ACOTAR, where everyone has at least a touch of darkness? Check out The Folk of the Air series by Holly Black. When Jude was a child, the father of her half-sister, the faerie Madoc, murdered her parents and took her back to the Faerie world with him. Raised as part of the gentry, Jude lives in a world where her mortal nature is hated and despised, but she battles for her place at court anyway while struggling with her love-hate relationship with her adoptive father and a growing bond with the titular prince, a relationship that is strictly forbidden. Jude is a fierce and extremely morally gray character, and one that fans of Feyre will adore.

Looking for more smart women at the center of beautifully-rendered fantasy stories? You’ll love Princess Lucero-Elisa de Riqueza of Orovalle, star of this series-starter by Rae Carson. Elisa was chosen for “Service” as a baby, when a godstone was placed in her navel by the gods, signaling that she was destined for greatness. But as a young woman, Elisa is self-hating and miserable. She’s never done anything even remotely great, and spends her time isolated, overweight, and reading military strategy books. One day she’s shocked to discover she’s been married off to the king of a distant land on the brink of war—and suddenly all that rage and book learning becomes invaluable as she struggles to survive an unfamiliar court and help her new homeland survive a dangerous onslaught.

If you loved Feyre’s journey as she discovered unknown reservoirs of power and courage inside herself, you should read Leigh Bardugo’s Grishaverse novels, starting with Shadow and Bone. As a child, Alina was tested by the Grisha and found to possess no magical ability. As an adult, she serves as a cartographer in the army. Charged with guiding the Darkling—the most powerful of the Grisha—across the dangerous and terrifying Shadow Fold, Alina is unexpectedly revealed to have incredible powers and is packed off to train with the Grisha. There, she must determine who her friends and enemies are, even while falling under the spell of the charismatic Darkling.

Emilia di Carlo and her sister Vittoria are very different—Emilia is bookish and shy, Vittoria outgoing and brash—but they share a secret: They’re both streghe, and have spent their lives learning to use magic. In this version of Italy, the Malvagi (the seven princes of Hell) haven’t been seen in a long time, but a terrifying accident summons the Prince of Wrath and leaves three witches dead, including Vittoria. Emilia swears to use her power to avenge her sister, but when her revenge is delayed and she’s forced to work with Wrath, unwanted feelings begin to tick up the spice level to an uncomfortable degree.

#3489. All 10 James Bond Movies Not Based On Ian Fleming's Books, Ranked

Though James Bond creator Ian Fleming's influence is still acutely felt with the long-running movie series adapting his literary character, the films have taken considerable creative liberties for decades. Adaptations of Fleming's work had grown significantly looser as early as the Sean Connery era, while many of the movies named after them still contained elements from the stories. A prime example is, despite "The Spy Who Loved Me" being plagued by copyright troubles, it still retained a villain with metal-capped teeth. But by the end of Roger Moore's lengthy tenure, the movies had largely ditched incorporating any of Fleming's elements, though that wasn't true of 2006's "Casino Royale."

We're taking a look back at the James Bond movies that are not based on Ian Fleming's books and short stories. Some of the entries here take their titles from short stories written by Ian Fleming but, frankly, nothing else. Outside of the inclusion of Bond and his usual allies and enemies, these cinematic narratives really strike out on their own creatively.

Here are all 10 James Bond movies not based on Ian Fleming's books ranked, going in their own direction with the super-spy.

Pierce Brosnan currently remains the only actor whose entire run as James Bond featured original narratives for his movies, rather than drawing directly from a specific Fleming story. In taking Bond out of the Cold War setting in which he originated, this led to an uneven tenure, despite Brosnan's best efforts. However, nothing could quite save Brosnan's last turn as 007 in 2002's "Die Another Day," opening with a title track by Madonna that sounded dated when it was released. The movie has Bond square off with a rogue North Korean general while trying to identify who betrayed him on a mission that led to a prolonged torturous imprisonment.

IMDb names "Die Another Day" as the worst James Bond movie, a dubious distinction that is, unfortunately, well-deserved. The movie opens with Bond infiltrating North Korea by surfing, because that's clearly what the kids are still into, and it only gets worse from there. This backslide into mediocrity spreads to the cinematography, complete with shoddy CG effects and random slow-motion sequences for no discernible reason other than an attempt to look cool. An absolute travesty and an embarrassing way for Brosnan to end his time as Bond, "Die Another Day" is a grating viewing experience.

Yes, "A View to a Kill," Moore's swan song to the franchise, takes its title from the 1960 Fleming short story "From a View to a Kill." But whereas the literary namesake features Bond hunting a motorcycle-driving assassin in France, the 1985 movie pits 007 against an immoral tech tycoon before it was cool. The tycoon in question is Max Zorin (Christopher Walken), a sadistic figure looking to corner the microchip market by destroying Silicon Valley. But outside of Walken chewing the scenery, joined by Grace Jones playing his enforcer, and a memorable title track by Duran Duran, the movie falls flat.

Roger Moore was horrified by "A View to a Kill," particularly the widespread casual violence, as Zorin mercilessly murders many of his associates. We're personally horrified by how rough around the edges the overall movie is, from its lackluster stunts to its abrupt finale. To make matters worse, when the movie's filming wrapped, at 57 years old, Moore looks visibly aged out of playing a spry secret agent. A half-hearted end to Moore's celebrated run playing James Bond, "A View to a Kill" feels as tired as its lead actor.

Daniel Craig's sophomore outing as Bond in 2008's "Quantum of Solace" also takes its title from a 1960 short story written by Fleming. But the literary tale simply follows Bond as he attends a dinner party in Nassau where he hears a story about an unhappy marriage. With that certainly not enough for an action movie to go off of, the film instead functions as a direct sequel to "Casino Royale," opening minutes later. Bond uncovers a global network that's infiltrated government organizations worldwide, including MI6, while contending with his own unresolved grief over his recently deceased lover Vesper Lynd (Eva Green).

For as much grief as "Quantum of Solace" gets, constantly existing in the shadow of "Casino Royale," it's a perfectly watchable Bond movie. The shortest in the series to date, the film does feel like a parade of action set pieces, but Craig's performance grounds the spectacle. The movie's themes about water scarcity and a cabal of affluent influencers trying to manipulate international governments does feel prescient. Coming off as an extended epilogue to "Casino Royale" rather than its own standalone experience, "Quantum of Solace" really works best watched in concert with its immediate predecessor.

Compared to its more action-oriented predecessor, "The World Is Not Enough" tried to lean more into dramatic territory. The 1999 movie opens with Bond (Brosnan) tricked into delivering a bomb to MI6 related to a kidnapping plot involving oil heiress Elektra King (Sophie Marceau). After being assigned to protect Elektra, Bond hunts down the terrorist responsible for the explosive incident, only to uncover a whole plot targeting vital oil pipelines into Europe. This leads Bond to realize that Elektra is not as helpless or innocent as he believed when they struck up their illicit romance.

Taking its title from Bond's family motto introduced in "On Her Majesty's Secret Service," "The World Is Not Enough" tries to feel like a more personal adventure for 007 accordingly. But as good a femme fatale as Sophie Marceau is, the movie never quite delivers on the emotional potential that it aspires to. The action is a bit lackluster too, feeling like something more akin to a theme park stunt spectacular than a blockbuster set piece. Underscoring that Brosnan was often working with lesser material during his Bond run, "The World Is Not Enough" couldn't live up to its creative ambitions.

There was a lot of expectation riding on "Spectre" after the critical and commercial success of its immediate predecessor "Skyfall." The movie also marks the first official Bond movie since "Diamonds Are Forever" to explicitly include Ernst Stavro Blofeld, after protracted legal issues prevented the villain's usage. This time, Blofeld is played by Christoph Waltz, with the added backstory that he and Bond grew up together contentiously as surrogate brothers, before the criminal mastermind faked his death. Since then, the movie reveals Blofeld has secretly been tormenting Bond from the shadows, leading to their eventual unhappy reunion for the fate of the world.

"Spectre" falls into the trap of trying to emulate "Skyfall" too much, right down to directly lifting music tracks from the preceding movie's score. The idea of Blofeld being Bond's brother figure, a concept also introduced in the 007 spoof "Austin Powers in Goldmember," is a laughable way to make their dynamic feel more personal. What salvages the movie from its lackluster script is its top-notch cinematography by Hoyte van Hoytema, particularly its stunning opening scene in Mexico City.

Brosnan's sophomore outing as Bond in 1997's "Tomorrow Never Dies" doesn't get as much credit as it deserves, overshadowed by its more successful predecessor. Another prescient entry in the series as far as its story is concerned, the main villain is a murderous media mogul providing his own news output. In order to take his media empire to the next level, Elliot Carver (Jonathan Pryce) tries to orchestrate a war between the United Kingdom and China. Bond and Chinese intelligence operative Wai Lin (Michelle Yeoh) work together to expose Carver's plot and prevent the conflict from breaking out.

Considering "Tomorrow Never Dies" scrapped its script days before filming, it's a wonder the movie came out as well as it did. The movie goes even more global than many other series' entries, taking Bond everywhere from Carver's offices in Germany to the streets of Saigon. What holds the movie back is that its plot does feel visibly rushed, while none of the action set pieces are as satisfying as the big moments in "GoldenEye." A glossier approach to the franchise than its predecessor's post-Cold War grittiness, "Tomorrow Never Dies" is a serviceable entry in Brosnan's Bond legacy.

When Daniel Craig closed out his celebrated run as James Bond, he did so with a bang, leaving no stone unturned. This made "No Time to Die" the longest James Bond movie ever, opening with Bond believing his latest serious paramour, Madeleine Swann (Léa Seydoux), had betrayed him to Spectre. After abruptly leaving the service in the wake of this assumption, Bond is pulled back into action when a secret weapon is stolen from the British government. In the process of destroying this deadly project, Bond has to face familiar faces from his life before a fatal showdown against the terrorist Lyutsifer Safin (Rami Malek).

While it could've trimmed about 15 minutes from its runtime, "No Time to Die" provides Craig with a largely solid farewell. From the dusty streets of Italy where Bond tries to get closure for the events of "Casino Royale" to its explosive finale, the movie hits all the right notes. The film's villains, including Malek's Safin, are a bit of a mixed bag, but the action, including a centerpiece sequence in Cuba, is competently staged. A satisfying end to Craig's five-movie run as 007, "No Time to Die" sticks the landing even if it takes some time to get there.

While it's not as fondly remembered today, 1989's "License to Kill" is an essential James Bond everyone should see at least once. Timothy Dalton's second and final turn as 007, the movie begins with Felix Leiter (David Hedison) and his new bride being attacked by drug lord Franz Sanchez (Robert Davi). With MI6 refusing to retaliate, considering the incident an outside matter, Bond angrily resigns from the service and sets out to avenge his friend. This unsanctioned vendetta eventually reveals that there is more at stake with Sanchez's latest scheme than Bond realized.

Though Dalton brought a more serious edge to Bond with his first movie in the role, "The Living Daylights," "License to Kill" is where he really cuts loose. Long before Daniel Craig did it, Dalton played Bond as a mean, lethal type that had no problem with getting his hands dirty to get the job done. These harder-edged sensibilities caught people off-guard, with the memory of the light-hearted Roger Moore tenure still fresh in their minds. But if you're looking to see why Timothy Dalton is filmmaker Christopher Nolan's favorite Bond actor, "License to Kill" is the perfect showcase.

After a six-year hiatus following "License to Kill," James Bond finally returned to the silver screen in 1995, this time with Pierce Brosnan playing the role. "GoldenEye" was almost the end of the James Bond franchise as it tried to find its way after the Cold War. The specter of those global tensions certainly inform the movie's story, with Bond learning a Soviet-era weapons satellite has been hijacked. Venturing into the heart of Russia to identify the culprit, Bond comes face-to-face with his old friend and former 00 Agent Alec Trevelyan (Sean Bean), now leading a crime syndicate.

The Bond movie series needed a shot of adrenaline if it hoped to stay alive after the Cold War, and "GoldenEye" delivered. Brosnan strikes the perfect balance between Moore's self-aware charm and Dalton's steely-eyed intensity while exploring the nuances of the character like never before. The action is as memorable as the franchise gets, and the supporting cast around Brosnan all turn in fantastic work, especially Bean as Trevelyan. Cementing the franchise's relevance beyond a set time period, "GoldenEye" remains the most important box office hit in Bond history, and that comes from a film of enduring quality.

Speaking of box office success, "Skyfall" became the biggest James Bond movie ever when it opened in theaters in 2012. Continuing Daniel Craig's run after a four-year hiatus, the movie has Bond reconcile with his lethal occupation's toll on his body and mind after a disastrous mission in Istanbul. Returning to duty after London is attacked by a shadowy figure linked to M (Judi Dench) and her own unresolved legacy, Bond has to contend with his own advancing age. Fortunately, this mission and its eccentric villain Raoul Silva (Javier Bardem) are just the things to help Bond overcome his midlife crisis.

Released in time for the film series' 50th anniversary, "Skyfall" feels like a celebration and commentary on the legacy of James Bond. Under sharp direction from Sam Mendes, the movie beautifully illustrates those themes while delivering bombastic action sequences, including a fantastic fight scene in Shanghai. Elevating the proceedings is haunting cinematography from Roger Deakins, really accentuating the light and shadows that Bond frequently plays in. An absolute masterpiece from top to bottom, "Skyfall" deconstructs Bond and thematically rebuilds him for the 21st century.

Rocky has returned to the big screen amid the 2026 movie schedule, but not in the way fans of the fictional boxer would’ve likely expected. Sylvester Stallone’s journey to getting the iconic 1976 film made is chronicled in the acclaimed biopic, I Play Rocky, which is helmed by Peter Farrelly. While Stallone had no direct involvement in the movie, he did give it his official stamp of approval to the creative team. However, the beloved actor accidentally sparked some serious drama after the movie was announced, and I was totally unaware of it.

As awards season heats up, the cast and creative team behind I Play Rocky have been making the rounds and promoting the movie. Farrelly recently took part in a wide-ranging discussion with Deadline as part of its Contenders series and reflected on making his latest flick. During the discussion, the Dumb and Dumber helmer spoke about receiving input from Stallone early on about his approach to his family, including his father, Frank Stallone Sr. Also, Sly and Farrelly agreed on a key detail that led the latter to make a request:

There’s a funny story. So, after he signed off, I said — we had the discussion [of] should he come on as a producer. I said, ‘Personally, I think you should not. I think it’s going to hurt you. Because you come across so great [in the film] and, at the end of the movie, if they see ‘executive-produced by Sylvester Stallone’ they’re going to think you shaped it,’ which he didn’t. And he agreed with that, and I said, ‘Just separate yourself a little from this.’

Honestly, the Oscar-winning filmmaker’s rationale (as shared on X) makes a lot of sense. If Stallone were credited as a producer on the film, which shows him in a mostly positive light, many may be tempted to think he manipulated the narrative. The Rambo star is, of course, no stranger to moviemaking so, given his directing and producing experience, I can see why he’d agree. Despite coming to an accord on Stallone needing to “separate” himself from the production, that apparently led to a serious faux pas on the actor’s part:

A week later, he’s doing an interview, and a guy says, ‘What do you think about this movie about the making of Rocky?’ And he goes, ‘I know nothing about it.’ And the internet goes crazy…. [People are like,] ‘These motherfuckers, they’re doing this movie without even going to Sylvester Stallone. Frank Stallone is threatening our lives, [Sly’s] brother. And Frank is like, ‘Can you believe these blah blah blah blah blah.’

The mere thought of getting heat from fans is daunting enough, but receiving heat from a member of the Stallone family is something else entirely. Farrelly went on to say that he later had another chat with the purveyor and lover of the Rocky films, and it went down as follows:

I called Sylvester [and] I go, ‘What are you doing?!’ He goes, ‘What?’ I said, ‘You said you knew nothing about it.’ He goes, ‘You said to separate myself.’ [I said,] ‘Not that far.’ And he says, ‘Oh okay, I will remember that going forward.’

I Thought Rocky And Creed's Big Fight Scene Would Be The End Of I Play Rocky. So What Happened?

While all this drama was due to a simple misunderstanding, it definitely created quite a mess for the filmmaking team. No lasting damage was seemingly done, though, and I’d say that things have been working out for Farrelly and his collaborators. The movie has been well received and gaining considerable buzz in the lead-up to the Oscars. It even received a stamp of approval from Ryan Gosling. As for Stallone, he admitted he was prepared to be “hypercritical” of the film, but he ended up really enjoying the movie as a whole and lead actor Anthony Ippolito’s portrayal of him.

I’d say that’s a generally happy ending to this story in the aftermath of the unintentional drama. Something I appreciate, though, is that Peter Farrelly is far enough removed from the situation that he can joke about it now. What isn’t a laughing matter, though, is the amount of heart that’s present in I Play Rocky, and fans can check out the film in theaters now.

#3486. Robert Pattinson's Divisive Sci-Fi Action Movie Proves He's Perfect For James Bond

How good does Robert Pattinson look in a tailored suit? Damn good, is the answer.

The proof is in Christopher Nolan's 2020 time-warp thriller "Tenet," wherein Pattinson sports a dazzling wardrobe of bespoke suits, knit polos, scarves, and impeccably rumpled pocket squares. The attire in "Tenet," provided by Oscar-nominated costume designer Jeffrey Kurland, are so impressive that GQ Magazine had to pause to write an article about them (even if it was just to complain that the suits look a little too good).

And, as we all know, looking good in a suit is one of the main requirements to play 007, so Pattinson has already passed his first test as our newly-cast James Bond.

However you feel about "Tenet," one has to admit that its costumes are amazing and that Pattinson rocks every single outfit he wears. He carries himself with poise and class, playing the sidekick Neil to the film's protagonist, The Protagonist (John David Washington). Poise and class are the bedrocks on which James Bond is built, and Pattinson can certainly handle those qualities with skill.

"Tenet" is Nolan's lowest-rated directorial effort among critics on Rotten Tomatoes, and in his own review for /Film, Chris Evangelista pointed out that no one will be able to figure out what the heck is going on in the film. Having seen it, I agree and can confirm that I have trouble grasping the physics of its sci-fi rigmarole. The movie centers on a machine that can cause people and objects to travel through time in "reverse," yet they continue to exist in regular space. As a result, humans and items that have been "inverted" seem to be moving in reverse. To them, though, it's the rest of the world that appears to be going in the wrong direction.

By the time-travel conceit of "Tenet," effect precedes cause. That means an inverted person can point a backward-moving gun at a target and, somehow, a bullet is sucked out of the wall and pulled back into the gun's chamber. How an inverted person caused that to happen is unclear to me. There is likewise a scene wherein the regular-moving Protagonist has to fight someone who is inverted and while Christopher Nolan's use of reverse photography is ingenious here, I couldn't help but wonder how one lands a punch when one is moving backward through time.

And if the time-travel physics are hard enough to fathom, there's also a twisted plot laid on top of them. The average sci-fi fan will likely be unable to remember all the details after just one go-through. Really, one will likely only recall a few fascinating visuals from "Tenet," and a very, very general sense of what's happening.

In short, Kenneth Branagh plays a dying Russian oligarch who has decided to destroy the world, with Robert Pattison and John David Washington playing the agents sent to foil his efforts. In addition, the oligarch's estranged wife (Elizabeth Debicki) is tragically mixed up in all this. The film even climaxes with armies of soldiers moving alternately forward and backward through time, and the apprehension of an oblique doomsday device. Truly, "Tenet" is a rather confusing movie.

Again, some of the imagery in "Tenet" is elaborate and fascinating, and the scenes of Neil and the Protagonist discussing things have a breezy tone. Even if their conversations are oblique and unmemorable, one gets the vibe that Pattinson is wholly at ease. He has a 007-like confidence.

As mentioned, "Tenet" might be Christopher Nolan's least beloved film. It's too hard-to-follow to be a super crowd-pleaser, and it wasn't as well-loved by the Academy as some of Nolan's other movies (despite winning the Oscar for Best Visual Effects). Some critics were downright savage to the film, including Mick LaSalle. Writing for the San Francisco Chronicle, he gave the film one star out of four, arguing that it was confusing yet didn't really inspire a viewer to try to understand it.

Brian Tallerico, writing for RogerEbert.com, was kinder, giving the film three stars out of four and drawing parallels to the James Bond franchise. He noted that Kenneth Branagh's destruction-hungry Russian oligarch is straight out of the Bond playbook, adding:

"[T]here's never been a Bond movie so stuffed with expository dialogue. 'Tenet' spends roughly two hours of its 150-minute run time explaining what is happening, why it is happening, and what might happen next. And yet even with that it's still incredibly difficult to follow because Nolan goes so far down his own rabbit hole of time travel that one almost needs to take notes to keep up (and I still think it arguably wouldn't all add up if they could)."

Still, Tallerico noted, "If 'Tenet' can be a hard movie to engage with emotionally or even comprehend narratively, that doesn't take away from its craftsmanship on a technical level." It is, many might agree, an impressive feat, even if it is opaque.

Robert Pattinson, meanwhile, has said that "Tenet" is not about time travel. Of course not. As we now know, the movie is just as much about spy vibes and nice suits as it is time inversion.

#3485. Go on a trip with Dave and Beezlebub for a sick boss fight in GTA 6

The Hell event in GTA 6 proves that you never know where a wild night in Leonidas can take you. On a quiet street, you might come across Dave and Beelzebub hanging out in a garage and listening to some rock. After a quick chat, you will learn that both of them are followers of Satan and enthusiasts of non-human vocalists in metal bands. If you stay around long enough, the two guys will invite you to take part in a special ritual, giving you the chance to start a unique event in the game.

If you're ready to explore unknown places, here's how to start the Hell event in GTA 6 and how to defeat the final boss.

To start the Hell event, you must meet Dave and Beelzebub at their garage on the north side of Port Hellhorn. The closest point of reference is Hank's Waffles to the northeast. You will know you have found the place once you see a house on the corner with the words "Welcome to the Hell hole" written on the wall. It's important to visit the place after starting Chapter 2, and at night, after 10 p.m. In our experience, whenever we visited the place earlier, the garage was closed.

Enter the garage, talk to the two guys and wait for a while. You can interact with them by accepting a beer or talking about music, but it's not necessary to progress the event. Eventually, a van will pull over. Dave will invite you to participate in a ritual to enter Satan's infernal dominion. To accept it, talk to Dave at the back of the van.

Once you are in control again, move to the campfire, hold L2/LT to look into the fire. This will teleport you to, well, Hell, where you start playing the minigame.

After completing the event, you can collect the Hellspawn Comshot, a unique weapon located beside the throne where you wake up. You're also rewarded with a new tattoo design, the Circles of Hell top, and a permanent max health upgrade.

At the third level in the Hell event, you will encounter the final boss. Throughout the battle, black goats will spawn and run in from the sides of the demon's throne. You want to avoid getting hit, so you can either kill the goats or dodge them.

Surviving is not your only concern during this fight. You must make the boss vulnerable to damage by destroying the bipedal, headless demons that appear in the arena. They explode when you kill them, so be sure to keep your distance. After killing at least one of them, the boss's health bar turns red, indicating that you can start shooting it. The effect lasts for a short time, so you will need to repeat this process a few times to complete the event.

#3484. These Are the Best Ways to Encrypt Your Email

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

As this in-depth explainer from Adaptive Security describes, most emails are encrypted in transit via Transport Layer Security (TLS), which prevents anyone from reading your message as it travels from server to server. However, encryption is temporarily stripped at each server: content is received and processed in plaintext and then re-encrypted when it leaves, meaning it could be read, logged, and distributed by the server provider.

Emails are also typically encrypted at rest—for example, while sitting on Google's servers and in a Gmail recipient's inbox. But this only prevents someone with physical access to the server hardware from reading messages, as Google still holds the encryption key and can access stored data. And, as PCMag points out, Google is scanning your messages to a degree, and it (along with other email providers) can and will hand emails over to law enforcement and government agencies in some cases.

If you have an account with a major email provider like Gmail, Outlook, or Apple Mail, you can add a third-party tool that layers an encryption protocol like OpenPGP on top of your existing account. PCMag recommends PreVeil, SecureMyEmail, and Virtru (which is limited to Gmail users in Chrome) for those who want to keep their current emails. Mailvelope is a browser add-on (and therefore a desktop-only tool) available in Chrome, Firefox, and Edge, though it can also be installed on other browsers, like Brave, that are built on the same architecture. FlowCrypt integrates with Gmail and Google Workspace on desktop and mobile.

Note that enterprise users of Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 have access to true end-to-end encryption without third-party add-ons. Gmail's Confidential mode and Outlook's Encrypt feature, available to all users, are not E2EE equivalents, as Google and Microsoft, respectively, still manage the keys.

For those who are willing to start fresh with a new email address (or who have a custom domain), providers like Proton Mail or Tuta offer native end-to-end encryption. The caveat: by default, this is only between users on the same service, so from one Proton user to another. If you want to send an end-to-end encrypted email from Proton to a Gmail user, for example, you have to set up password protection (and share the password via another secure channel) or use a PGP-compatible tool like those listed above. You can also Proton's Gmail integration does allow for end-to-end encryption, but only if both Gmail parties are using the Proton integration.

#3483. OpenAI upgrades ChatGPT and Codex with new GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol models

OpenAI kicked off the GPT-6 generation with Astra in September, then upgraded Sol to GPT-6.1 a few weeks later at DevDay.

Today, GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol are coming to ChatGPT Work and Codex together. OpenAI says both can finish demanding tasks with fewer output tokens, so you can get more done before hitting your usage limit.

Astra is still the model OpenAI recommends for your hardest projects.

Say you have a screenshot of a slide and want the rest of your presentation to look like it. OpenAI says GPT-6.2 Astra can use that screenshot as a template and match the layout, colors, and even the font size.

On the Codex side, OpenAI says Astra is better at making and testing changes in an existing project.

“Early testers reported cleaner code style and more focused tests, with fewer rounds of revision,” OpenAI says.

Sol is the more affordable model for everyday coding and writing, and it gets surprisingly close to Astra on one coding test.

Cognition’s FrontierCode 2.0 measures whether changes to real codebases are good enough for maintainers to merge.

With both models at maximum reasoning effort, OpenAI says Sol came within half a point of Astra at about one-fifth the cost.

Some of you have been asking very politely. Some of you have just been asking.GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol are now available.Super efficient and built to perform where it counts—the real world.https://t.co/qr2iP0GpfX pic.twitter.com/jLCyVIws2Y

Both models are available starting today in ChatGPT Work and Codex on Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu.

The $200/month Pro plan also gets Ultrafast mode for the first time with Sol. The $500/month Pro plan gets Ultrafast on both models, as do eligible Enterprise and Edu workspaces once an admin enables it.

How fast is Ultrafast? OpenAI says it can generate tokens at up to 4.5 times the standard rate on either model, although it uses more of your allowance. You can switch speeds from the model picker.

Developers can use both models through the API today as well. Astra’s standard input and output prices are 20% lower than with GPT-6 Astra, while Sol keeps its GPT-6.1 pricing.

Warning! Spoilers ahead for the Season 10 fall finale of 9-1-1, “Et Tu?,” which is available to stream with a Hulu subscription.

9-1-1 has officially wrapped up the first half of its 10th season on the 2026 TV schedule, and it was anything but calm. Thursday’s fall finale included some intense calls, and even more intense scenes between Buck and Eddie as their latest fallout continues. The best friends have not really been on the same page for a while now, and I’ve been worried about them. Luckily, the executive producer is explaining where things stand with them following the midseason finale.

Buck’s big decision in the Season 9 finale to foster his biological son following the death of his parents has led to some difficulties at the start of Season 10. The toddler, Theo, is a bit rambunctious and doesn’t take well to authority. This has put a strain on Buck’s relationship with Eddie, who knows what it’s like to be a single father. It doesn’t help that after Buck decided to give Theo up, Eddie became his foster dad through emergency placement. This has put even more pressure on them, and EP and showrunner Tim Minear told TV Insider why they went in this direction:

I think conflict is drama, obviously, but it felt… To me, it was sort of an interesting way to have Eddie come in and take Buck’s story away from him in a sense. They both have stories, right? Obviously, Theo is Buck’s biological kid. Buck had every good intention of fostering and growing into that role, which he still has an opportunity to do. But also, I just believe that Eddie would not let that kid go into a group home. And I think there was some truth in what Buck said about Eddie’s guilt about being ambivalent about his own son in the first five years of his life.

Buck had donated sperm to his friend and his wife, who were having trouble conceiving a few seasons ago, and after helping her deliver, it didn’t really come up again...until last season. Then, after the couple died in a car crash, Buck felt responsible for the kid and took him in. There was some concern for Buck going into Season 10, and it was obvious this wasn’t going to be easy, especially after seeing Theo’s chaotic energy. So he ultimately believed that Theo would be better with someone else.

However, Minear is right in believing that Eddie, who was the only one who knew what Buck was doing, wouldn’t let Theo go to a group home. Unfortunately, this creates more conflict between them, but it’s what makes the situation more realistic:

So again, a lot of the stories here this season — look, we’re in Season 10, and a lot of the stories this season are an accumulation of canon that we’ve built up over the past decade with these characters. And that always makes for a richer story, it seems to me. But I actually think Buck and Eddie, conflict is natural, particularly between people who are really close. Nobody can piss you off as much as someone who you’re really close to, and I just think that’s real.

Despite the growing tension in the midseason finale, Buck and Eddie had somewhat made up towards the end of the episode. While Buck wasn’t quite ready to see Theo, he understood why Eddie did what he did. It’s hard to tell where things will go for them in the new year, but with Theo staying with Eddie and Buck coming to terms with everything, it should be interesting. On that note, Minear shares that both of them will have some growing to do for multiple reasons:

Yeah, I think they’re at an interstitial stage where Buck sees that it is really best for Theo right now to be with Eddie. Maybe neither one of them handled it perfectly, but if they handled it perfectly, then you’d have a five-episode season as opposed to 18. But I think they’re in a good place in their friendship. I think that Theo becomes a spoiler a little bit, and until Buck feels like he can walk into that house and face that kid, there’s kind of a natural barrier there between whatever kind of closeness that he can enjoy with Eddie off the job.

I have been worried about Buck and Eddie’s relationship since the beginning of the season, when it was clear that Buck fostering Theo would bring some problems. And it didn’t get any easier when Eddie became the foster parent. I’m definitely glad that they’ve crossed a barrier, and they both realize how they acted in this situation might not have been the best. However, I am looking forward to seeing what happens now that they have an understanding with each other and Theo.

9-1-1 is now on its winter hiatus, but the series will return on Thursday, January 7 at 8 p.m. ET on ABC, streaming the next day on Hulu.

#3481. Mads Mikkelsen And Eva Green Had A James Bond Reunion In An R-Rated Western Movie

After landing his breakthrough Hollywood role as the blood-weeping baddie Le Chiffre in "Casino Royale," it seemed like Mads Mikkelsen would be a go-to villain for years to come. He was horrifyingly seductive as Dr. Hannibal Lecter in the NBC series "Hannibal," at which point it was hard to see mainstream viewers accepting him as anything other than a straight-up monster.

I don't know that he's turned the corner with American audiences, but there's ample evidence out there for moviegoers willing to go off the beaten path that Mikkelsen is terrifically effective as a hero. He can even be downright lovable, as he is in Thomas Vinterberg's booze-drenched comedy "Another Round" (where he gets to show off his hoofing chops).

Mikkelsen is not anywhere close to loveable in Kristian Levring's 2014 Western "The Salvation," but he is brutally compelling as a Danish combat veteran who settles east of the Mississippi River in the 1860s, and goes to war with a malevolent crime boss played with vicious glee by Jeffrey Dean Morgan. It's a different kind of role for Mikkelsen, and a departure for his "Casino Royale" co-star Eva Green as well. Whereas she was glamorous and wounded as Vesper Lynd, she's just flat-out wounded as Morgan's serially abused sister-in-law.

Levring conjures the widescreen majesty of Sergio Leone (replete with an Ennio Morricone-esque score), and depicts the violence with a matter-of-fact bluntness. Alas, despite receiving mostly good reviews (it holds a 72% Fresh rating at Rotten Tomatoes), it got unceremoniously dumped into U.S. theaters in 2015. It's currently available to stream on multiple services, so now is the time to catch up with it!

Mikkelsen stars as Jon, who leaves Denmark with his brother Peter (Mikael Persbrandt) to start anew in America. Eventually, Jon's wife (Nanna Øland Fabricius) and son (Toke Lars Bjarke) join him, and the trio sets out on a stagecoach to begin the American chapter of their lives. Their hopes and dreams are immediately shattered when two criminals eject Jon from the stagecoach. The rape and kill his wife, and also murder his son.

Jon tracks down the coach, and kills the two men. That's revenge served piping hot, but it causes new troubles for Jon, as one of the murderers was the brother of ruthless gang leader Henry Delarue (Morgan). Delarue flies into a rage and begins killing townspeople, hoping to intimidate them into helping him capture Jon. Delarue's savagery knows no bounds, and he's especially fond of inflicting his cruelty on Green's mute Madelaine.

Levring isn't out to reinvent the genre. He just wants to make a good-and-bloody Western where the truly nasty bad guys get theirs before the credits roll. If you're a fan of the genre, this is a solid programmer filled with superb performances. So saddle up and get your gunslinging fix. (And then catch up with one of Mikkelsen's finest performances in "The Hunt").

#3480. 10 Privacy Hacks Every Mac User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Enabling the macOS Firewall (which is off by default) adds a layer of protection against external devices on your wifi network, as well as unauthorized apps from initiating a connection to your device. Turning on Stealth Mode prevents your Mac from even responding to these requests, essentially making it invisible to anything that's scanning a network you're connected to. This makes it more difficult for hackers and malware to know your device exists, much less attack it. This can interfere with certain essential activity when you're on your home network, but it's a valuable security setting when on public wifi. You can leave Firewall on all the time and enable Stealth Mode only as needed. Go to Settings > Network > Firewall, flip the toggle, then hit Options to manage Stealth Mode.

Images and screenshots contain metadata, such as timestamps, device and hardware details, and, in the case of photos, physical location. Much of this information is stripped automatically when you share files to social media or via encrypted messaging apps, but if you're sending them via text or email, posting to forums, or sharing over AirDrop, metadata remains intact. You can easily remove metadata from your images right on your desktop. Select the file and hit control + click to bring up an options menu, then go to Quick Actions > Convert Image. Uncheck the box next to Preserve Metadata, then hit Convert. (This is also useful for quickly converting HEIC to JPEG without opening a separate app.)

If you're using iCloud to store photos, files, and device backups, your data is encrypted on Apple's servers and in transit. Apple still holds the decryption key, which is useful if you somehow get locked out of your account and need help recovering it, but for sensitive data—including device backups—end-to-end encryption is the most secure way to ensure no one but you can gain access. Advanced Data Protection is an opt-in setting for iCloud that encrypts your information end to end. You'll need to set up an alternative recovery method, such as your device passcode with two-factor authentication, a recovery contact, or a recovery key. Be careful, though: If you lose access to this recovery method, you will lose your data. You can enable Advanced Data Protection on your Mac under System Settings > [Your Name] > iCloud > Advanced Data Protection > Turn On. Note that some iCloud data, including passwords and payment methods, are already end-to-end encrypted by default.

#3478. Robert Redford And Scarlett Johansson's '90s Disney Neo-Western Movie Is Worth Revisiting

Nicholas Evans' "The Horse Whisperer" was a publishing phenomenon in 1995. The novel is about a young girl who's involved in a horseback riding accident that kills her best friend and their horse, leaving her and her own horse seriously injured. When she falls into a deep funk, her mother whisks her off to rural Montana. There, they try to heal her horse emotionally via a horse whisperer. And while she is married, the mother finds herself falling in love with the handsome, deeply sensitive animal shrink, something which, according to many critics, transformed the narrative into a shamelessly sentimental romance à la "The Bridges of Madison County."

The novel sold millions of copies, which meant a film adaptation was inevitable. Like "The Bridges of Madison County," the pedigree didn't make it immediately attractive to A-list directors. But Robert Redford saw something more in the material and took it on as his first directorial effort since his brilliant 1994 drama "Quiz Show." For the first time in his filmmaking career, Redford took the lead in his own movie. He also assembled a sensationally talented cast that included Kristin Scott Thomas, Dianne Wiest, Sam Neill, Chris Cooper, and Cherry Jones. For the role of the young girl, he and the casting team of Ellen Chenoweth and Gretchen Rennell went with up-and-comer Scarlett Johansson, who gave a moving performance that wound up being her breakthrough role.

"The Horse Whisperer" isn't quite on the level of the movie version of "The Bridges of Madison County" (a lovely film that Clint Eastwood saved from production limbo), but the screenplay credited to Eric Roth and Richard LaGravenese is nuanced in a way that maybe the novel isn't. And though it's not one of Redford's best movies, it's a strong piece of work that deserves more attention.

"The Horse Whisperer" holds a 72% Fresh critical approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes and grossed $187 million at the worldwide box office upon hitting theaters. That was a decent result for Touchstone Pictures, but it didn't come close to matching the runaway success of its source material.

Robert Redford rarely failed to strike up chemistry with his leading ladies ("The Great Gatsby" being a notable exception), so it's hardly a shocker that he's perfectly paired with Kristin Scott Thomas. This is not, however, a heated attraction, as Redford's character is still mourning the end of a previous romance where the woman chose the city over him and the country. Thomas is from the city, too (and, again, married), so he's worried that another heartbreak is around the corner.

As for Scarlett Johansson, she captures the grief of a young woman whose life has been irreparably changed. Her leg was partially amputated, which she fears will make her undesirable to romantic partners as she gets older. This gives rise to the most overpoweringly emotional scene in the movie when, after a row with her mother, Johansson's character tearfully asks, "Who's going to want me?" If that doesn't switch on your waterworks, go straight to the doctor, because your heart isn't properly functioning.

"The Horse Whisperer" is available to rent via streaming, but the film is badly in need of a digital restoration. Hopefully, Disney will commission one at some point, although I'm not sure if the movie is a popular enough library title to merit such treatment.

#3477. If Your Google Pixel's Camera Is Suddenly Broken, Here's the Fix

Updates are generally good for your devices. The latest Chrome update, for example, patches an actively exploited security vulnerability, while Apple's latest updates stop people from seeing iMessages they shouldn't have access to. In most cases, it's beneficial to update your tech to the latest software version whenever possible.

Sadly, updates aren't all perfect, as Google Pixel users are discovering this week. As reported by Android Authority, Google's November update apparently shipped with a bug that breaks some Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 cameras. Seeing as Pixels are rather famous for their shooters, this is a decidedly unfortunate glitch.

Here's the situation: Following the November update, some users are opening their Pixel Camera apps to find an error that reads, "Something went wrong. Close and open the Camera app again," with a "Learn More" link to, well, learn more. Others aren't receiving the error, but are instead running into a blank Camera viewfinder, as if the lens is totally covered. What's more, some users are reportedly saying that the issue is present on third-party camera apps, not just the Pixel Camera app. That would imply this is an issue with the camera system-wide, not just the Pixel Camera app itself.

To be clear, it doesn't seem like this is a universal issue. It's not like all Pixel users are now running with broken cameras. But based on the forum complaints Android Authority discovered, it seems reasonable to assume that this glitch isn't limited to just a handful of unlucky Pixel owners.

Luckily, there is an apparent workaround here, though it's not totally obvious. Some users are having no luck restarting their Pixels, while others report that a factory reset wasn't enough to restore camera functionality.

What does appear to work, however, is shutting your Pixel down and waiting five minutes or so. It's not clear why, but giving your Pixel a chance to "breathe" seems to shake the glitch and bring back your camera. As Android Authority reports, that fix comes from "Diamond and Gold product experts" on Google's Support forum.

If your Pixel's camera is giving you grief following the November update, this workaround is definitely worth a try—especially since more drastic measures don't actually seem to do anything. As the issue does seem to be rather widespread, I wouldn't be surprised to see Google issue a patch in the coming days. But until then, turning your phone off for five minutes may be a decent compromise.

#3476. American Psycho Reboot Is 'Not Happening,' Director Says

We won't be getting a new take from the director of Challengers

A couple of years ago, reports emerged that Challengers and Call Me By Your Name director Luca Guadagnino was working on his own reimagining of American Psycho, the 2000 film adaptation of Bret Easton Ellis' novel. Unfortunately (or fortunately, depending on your point of view), it doesn't appear his new take on the cult-hit psychological thriller will see the light of day.

Luca Guadagnino was first linked to a new American Psycho adaptation written by Contagion's Scott Z. Burns in October 2024. We had not heard much more about the project since then, so Deadline asked Guadagnino about it during the director's recent appearance on its Crew Call podcast. Sadly, Guadagnino did not have a positive update on the project.

“Scott Z. Burns wrote a fantastic script. Unfortunately for me, as we speak, it’s not happening," Guadagnino succinctly explained.

American Psycho is a horror novel originally released in 1991, but it's mostly remembered for Mary Harron's 2000 film adaptation starring Christian Bale. The movie, which explores themes of toxic masculinity and materialism, was a subversive horror comedy for its time. Despite its very grim subject matter, Bale's over-the-top performance and key scenes from the movie have nestled their way into pop culture and become memes in the 26 years since the original's release. Even official accounts for kid-friendly franchises like Pokémon have referenced it.

Any new adaptation will have lofty expectations to live up to and will likely have to face the reality that many of the things the book lampoons have only gotten worse in the decades since its original release. Sadly, it looks like we'll never quite know how Guadagnino and Burns planned to reinterpret American Psycho for the modern day.

This new rendition of American Psycho isn't the only Luca Guadagnino project that hasn't come to fruition in recent years. He was attached to direct a movie based on Sgt. Rock for DC Studios, but that project was shelved before it could start shooting in 2025. Artificial, a movie about the founders of OpenAI, will be the next Guadagnino film to hit theaters. It'll be released on Dec. 25.

#3475. Why iPhone Duo wasn’t for me (but might be for you)

I’ve had the iPhone Duo for nearly two weeks now, and have officially decided to return it. Here are the three main reasons why the Duo didn’t work out for me, but might for you.

I use my iPhone one-handed all the time, and based on my experience, iPhone Duo is clearly intended to be used with two hands. You can use it one-handed, but for me it’s not nearly as comfortable as the iPhone 18 Pro. It’s too wide and too heavy to be used for long.

Perhaps over time I’d get used to needing two hands for most iPhone interactions. But that would be a pretty significant shift for me, as there are so many situations when I don’t have both hands free.

If you already use two hands with your iPhone regularly—perhaps because you have a Pro Max model—then the Duo’s one-handed experience likely won’t bother you. But the more I used the Duo, the more I found myself missing my iPhone 18 Pro.

The biggest value proposition of a foldable is that it’s a 2-in-1 product, letting you have a standard phone but also a tablet-sized display that fits in your pocket.

I totally get the appeal, and fully expected to love that hybrid design. But after two weeks of trying, I still struggled to find times when I actually wanted to unfold the Duo. And to be clear, that’s a me problem, not an issue with the Duo itself.

I tried a bunch of apps on the inner display, and struggled to find use cases that—for me—made it worthwhile to open the Duo. But based on the feedback I’ve seen from most Duo owners, I’m very much in the minority.

I know lots of people love the Duo for video, but I don’t watch much video on my iPhone. I almost never watch YouTube, TikTok, or Instagram Reels. And for shows and movies, I stick with my TV screen and an Apple TV 4K.

Multitasking support on iPhone Duo works really well. But when I found myself needing to multitask, I still reached for my iPad Pro with Magic Keyboard attached. A keyboard-free product can’t replace my main computer (nor would I expect it to), and the Duo screen was too small to comfortably work on it.

Last year I bought an iPhone Air and absolutely loved it. Initially, the Air’s less capable camera system didn’t bother me, it was “good enough.”

After a few months though, I started missing the Pro camera system more. Then I learned that my wife was pregnant with twins, and I knew I wanted the best possible iPhone cameras to capture their early weeks and months. So I bought an iPhone 18 Pro in September.

I’ve been very impressed by iPhone 18 Pro’s Main camera upgrades, and it’s great having a Telephoto lens again too. Since having the best camera system is so crucial for me right now, I knew iPhone Duo couldn’t be my only iPhone.

I initially planned to dual-carry the two models, using iPhone 18 Pro solely as a camera. But over and over I found myself wishing it was my only iPhone.

I returned mine as well. Beautiful device, but functionally not very good.

Is the iPhone Duo camera good enough for most people? Probably so. But for this year at least, with my twins aging rapidly, it’s not quite right for me. If I loved the Duo for other reasons, I would just use both models. But since I didn’t, I’m happy to stick with the iPhone 18 Pro.

In closing, I want to explicitly state that I don’t think the iPhone Duo is a bad product, and this isn’t a “bad review.”

The iPhone Duo just isn’t for me. I get the sense, though, that it’s lots of people’s favorite iPhone in years. Apple created its most unique new iPhone model since the original, and there’s plenty to love about it. I’m very curious to see how popular foldables become over time compared to slab models, because each clearly offers pros and cons. But for me, at least right now, the iPhone 18 Pro is my model of choice.

What has your iPhone Duo experience been like so far? Love it? Undecided? Let us know in the comments.

#3474. Why Wiress From The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Looks So Familiar

This article contains spoilers for "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping."

The original "Hunger Games" raised the stakes for Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence) and Peeta Mellark (Josh Hutcherson) by establishing that tributes from their home, District 12, have only ever won the Hunger Games twice in 74 years. That means they only have one mentor, the alcoholic Haymitch Abernathy (Woody Harrelson), unlike other Districts' tributes that have two mentors each.

"Hunger Games" author Suzanne Collins told the story of the first District 12 victor in "The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes" — Lucy Gray Baird (Rachel Zegler), who won the 10th Hunger Games decades before Katniss was born and then vanished. Now, "Sunrise on the Reaping" tells how Haymitch won his own Hunger Games.

Haymitch was at a disadvantage before he even entered the arena, since there were no District 12 victors available to mentor him. To address this issue, the Capitol "borrowed" victors from other districts and assigned them to mention Haymitch and his fellow District 12 tributes. Those mentors are Mags Flanagan (Lili Taylor) and Wiress (Maya Hawke), younger versions of characters who first appeared in the second "Hunger Games" film/book, "Catching Fire."

Wiress (played by Amanda Plummer back in "Catching Fire") isn't in the movie much, but "Hunger Games" fans will likely recognize the actress playing her. The daughter of Ethan Hawke and Uma Thurman, Maya Hawke is one of the more charming "nepo babies" to come out of recent Hollywood.

Hawke has been acting in film and television since 2017, when she played Jo March in a BBC production of "Little Women." In 2019, she not only appeared in Quentin Tarantino's "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" as "Flower Child," a member of the Manson family; she also got her big break. Hawkey joined "Stranger Things" in its third season as Robin Buckley, working alongside Steve Harrington (Joe Keery) at mall ice cream store Scoops Ahoy.

The season seems to set up Robin and Steve as a new romantic couple ... until she reveals she's not into guys! Despite the show taking place in the 1980s, though, Steve is cool with it. While Season 3 of "Stranger Things" tends to be remembered as one of its weaker outings, Robin was a great addition to the ensemble and Hawke returned as part of the main cast for the subsequent two seasons.

Hawke has also worked alongside her father. In historical miniseries "The Good Lord Bird," where Ethan Hawke starred as radical abolitionist John Brown, Maya Hawke played Brown's daughter, Annie. When Ethan Hawke directed the Flannery O'Connor biopic "Wildcat" in 2023, he cast Maya as the famed author.

Maya Hawke's other film roles include parts in Wes Anderson's "Asteroid City," Pixar sequel "Inside Out 2" as the voice of Anxiety, and a part in the upcoming "Magic: The Gathering" film. Hawke is also a singer-songwriter and has released four studio albums ("Blush," "Moss," "Chaos Angel," and "Maitreya Corso") as of 2026.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is now in theaters.

#3473. AirPods Pro 3 keep getting better, here’s what’s new in iOS 27

AirPods got a variety of new features this fall in iOS 27, several of which are exclusive to AirPods Pro 3 (now only $179). Here’s everything new.

Custom EQ is a feature that some AirPods users thought Apple would never ship, but iOS 27 adds it.

With Custom EQ, Apple now lets you set your own sound profile for AirPods. Per Apple:

AirPods are designed and engineered by Apple to faithfully represent music, TV shows and movies, and calls. If you prefer a different sound profile, you can customize how AirPods represent any audio played.

You can change the EQ by going to your AirPods’ settings ⇾ Audio & Routing ⇾ Equalizer ⇾ Custom. From here, you can adjust the sound profile for low, mid, and high frequencies.

Custom EQ is available on AirPods Pro 3, AirPods Pro 2, AirPods Max 2, AirPods 5, and AirPods 4.

Apple GymKit has been available for years, but only for Apple Watch. It lets you pair and sync workout data with compatible cardio equipment, like treadmills, ellipticals, indoor bikes, and more.

In iOS 27, GymKit expands to support iPhone using AirPods Pro 3’s heart rate sensor. My colleague Zac gave it a try:

The setup is simple. I tapped my iPhone to the treadmill, picked Indoor Walk (Indoor Run is also offered), and started the workout from the treadmill. With GymKit, workout data is stored privately on iPhone and removed from the equipment.

Once the workout started, the treadmill received heart-rate data from AirPods Pro 3. Meanwhile, the Fitness app on iPhone received the treadmill’s distance, pace, incline, and calorie data. Treadmills know details that an iPhone and AirPods can’t know on their own, especially incline and precise belt distance.

Siri AI is available on compatible iPhone hardware in iOS 27, and Apple made sure to expand full support for the AI assistant to AirPods too.

AirPods are essentially becoming an AI wearable thanks to the new Siri. It will let users do a lot more than the current Siri. Here are some key features via Apple’s website:

Earlier this year when AirTag 2 launched, Apple brought Precision Finding support to Apple Watch for the first time. Until now though, it’s been limited to AirTag 2.

But with iOS 27 and watchOS 27, Apple expands Precision Finding on the Watch to AirPods Pro 3.

AirPods Pro 3’s case includes the latest second-generation Ultra Wideband (UWB) chip, letting you find it with greater precision and step-by-step guidance right from your wrist.

With every batch of new AirPods features that debuts, the AirPods settings screen in the Settings app gets more cluttered.

But in iOS 27, Apple has a welcome fix: it’s redesigned and reorganized all AirPods settings.

Now, you’ll find AirPods settings organized into more categories and submenus, accompanied by colorful icons. It makes finding the right setting way easier and more intuitive than before.

#3472. Dustin Hoffman's Forgotten HBO Drama Series Was Canceled For A Tragic Reason

HBO launched on November 8, 1972, and has since produced some of the finest shows in television history. It has also produced plenty of swiftly forgotten and overlooked curios, many of which are actually quite good. The Dustin Hoffman-led "Luck" was, according to critics at least, one example. This horse racing drama looked set to be another ongoing hit for the network until it was canceled following the deaths of three horses involved in production, bringing a tragic end to the show despite the fact it had already been renewed.

David Milch began his career on "Hill Street Blues" before co-creating one of the best shows of the 1990s in "NYPD Blue." That alone would be enough to make him a TV legend, but Milch wasn't done. He managed to steer clear of the ill-advised "NYPD Blue" spin-off "Public Morals," which was canceled after one episode, but he did oversee his share of short-lived crime series in "Brooklyn South," "Total Security," and "Big Apple." It wasn't until 2004 that he struck gold again with the HBO series "Deadwood," arguably the best Western TV show ever made. After that, however, Milch's career involved creating little-known series that came and went without making much of an impact.

His 2006 series, "John from Cincinnati," was a strange affair that lasted just one season. "Luck," on the other hand, looked as though it could break the trend and go the distance. Set in the world of horse racing, the Hoffman-fronted series also benefited from the directorial talents of none other than Michael Mann, and became a critical hit, earning a second season renewal. But that second season never materialized after some unfortunate on-set events which forced HBO to cancel "Luck" despite the fact filming had already started on Season 2.

"Luck" was somewhat of a passion project for David Milch, who told the Los Angeles Times, "I've been thinking about doing a show like this for 25 years." The creator explained how his father had taken him to horse racing events since he was age five or six, and how he saw the horses as "heart-stopping beautiful." All of which just makes the story of "Luck" even more tragic.

Dustin Hoffman plays Chester "Ace" Bernstein, a gambler who after coming home after a three-year stay in federal prison immediately concocts a plan for revenge against those who helped put him away. His bodyguard, driver, and right hand man, Gus (Dennis Farina) acts as front for Ace's investment in race horse Pint of Plain. Meanwhile, Hoffman's gambler sets out to restore the failing Santa Anita racetrack as part of his plan for retribution. Nick Nolte also appears as a veteran trainer who now owns his own colt.

"Luck" premiered in January 2012 to positive reviews and looked as though it might have the potential to become one of the best HBO shows of all time. By the end of that month, the show had already earned a second season renewal. On January 31, 2012, the Los Angeles Times reported that HBO had ordered a further 10 episodes that were set to debut in January 2013, with production on the new season set to get underway in February. According to the outlet, the debut episode brought in 1.1 million viewers and the renewal was "hardly shocking" given Hoffman and Nolte's involvement. What was shocking, however, was that on March 14, 2012, the Los Angeles Times once again reported on the show, this time to announce it had been canceled altogether.

"Luck" Season 1 earned an 82% certified fresh rating on Rotten Tomatoes, with critics praising the cast and writing in particular. But behind all this success, there was trouble brewing. People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA) had been on top of HBO and "Luck" since January 2012, the month in which the show debuted. According to The Hollywood Reporter, the organization had written to the channel to enquire as to the treatment of horses used in the show, and had followed up on numerous occasions thereafter.

As a report from PETA explains, two horses were euthanized during production of the first season. According to the group, "older, arthritic horses had been used in dangerous (and deadly) racing sequences" leading to the two euthanizations. What's more, the report cites "insiders at Santa Anita Race Track" as having provided information about a third horse that died on-set. Rather than push on, HBO pulled the plug and "Luck" was added to the expansive list of the best shows canceled after only one season.

A statement from HBO (via the LA Times), read, "It is with heartbreak that executive producers David Milch and Michael Mann together with HBO have decided to cease all future production on the series 'Luck.'" The network claimed to have maintained "the highest safety standards throughout production," but acknowledged that "accidents unfortunately happen and it is impossible to guarantee they won't in the future." "Luck" Season 1 continued to air, but production on Season 2 was brought to an end despite plenty of footage having already been shot. Today, Season 1 remains available on HBO Max.

#3471. The Best GTA 6 Easter Eggs We’ve Seen So Far

Familiar faces (and voices) in unexpected places

Grand Theft Auto 6 is finally in the wild, and there are a mind-boggling number of things to do in Leonida. Many of them are terribly dangerous, like stealing cars from the police impound lot, getting into high-speed chases, and laundering stolen goods. But GTA 6 has plenty of wild and wacky optional activities too, many of which include references to pop-culture icons, past Rockstar games, or well-known memes. Here are a few of the coolest Easter eggs we've discovered in our own playthroughs and from other players on social media.

GTA's radio stations have become famous for their celebrity hosts over the years, and GTA 6 doubles down on that tradition. Weird Al is a host on Vice City FM, which plays 1980s hits from artists like Hall and Oates, Phil Collins, and Flock of Seagulls. He confirmed his role in the game in a recent Bluesky post, where he wrote, "I’m the host of GTA 6’s “non-stop ‘80s” radio channel Vice City FM. I also wrote some in-game commercials, and I’m the voice of the Burger Shot ads as well! As a long-time fan of the Grand Theft Auto franchise, I couldn’t be more excited about this. Okay, gotta get back to playing the game!"

During Jason's final days as a bachelor early in the game, one of the most relaxing activities you can get up to is swimming near his house. If you manage to venture out far enough, you'll come across an unusual watersports enthusiast: a German Shepherd riding a jet ski all by himself. This is likely a reference to a real dog in Fort Lauderdale, a Golden Retriever who's become a local attraction due to his love of riding the waves. The breeds may not be the same, but the shout-out is clear.

In Brian's office at the Marina, you can find a copy of a book called The Cowboy's Prayer Is to Die Young. It contains several references to the events of 2018's Red Dead Redemption 2, the previous game from GTA 6 developer Rockstar Games. The book follows protagonist Rust McCreary, a clear stand-in for Arthur Morgan, as he "rides across the final days of the West in a bloody quest for inner peace." If you flip through the pages, you'll find references to New Austin, Blackwater, and Ambarino. There's even a pretty detailed rundown of a main-story mission from RDR2, where Arthur tracks down gunslinger Flaco Hernandez to a cabin on Cairn Lake.

Once you make it to Port Gellhorn, you can find a convincing replica of Arthur's hat at a yard sale. The house is located about two blocks south of Moses' garage, so keep an eye out for signs.

Dexter, the beloved Showtime crime drama that aired between 2006 and 2013, takes place in Miami. So it's a natural fit for some kind of cameo in GTA 6. Near the top of Washington Island in Vice City, you'll find the Trinity Apartments, named in homage to one of the show's most memorable villains. The building itself is also a near-exact dupe of Dexter's own residence. If you venture into the building, you'll discover "Dexter's apartment" right where you'd expect it to be based on its location in the show. From there, explore the rooftop to find some of the noble serial killer's tools hidden up there, including a rope, a knife, and a syringe.

Leonida's radio stations feature plenty of recognizable voices, but there's one that's easy to miss. The Kaleidoscope channel features retro synth-pop, European disco, non-English covers of iconic '80s tunes, and plenty of deep cuts from Germany. The station is hosted by "DJ Dicky," but that velvety British baritone comes from none other than Jeremy Irons, the voice of Scar in The Lion King and the dastardly Simon Gruber in Die Hard With a Vengeance, along with countless other roles in film and television.

The Fast and the Furious series has no shortage of incredibly cool cars, but few are quite as memorable as the neon-green Mitsubishi Eclipse Paul Walker's Brian drives in the film that started it all. It has a sky-high rear spoiler and eye-catching blue body art, and you can get one of your own in GTA 6 by breaking into the garage on Vespucci Island. The location can be found in the middle of the Rialto Islands and west of Vice Beach.

Fans of Miami Vice director Michael Mann are probably already pretty pumped to spend dozens of hours in GTA 6, and now they've got another reason to celebrate. Rockstar's latest also includes an optional encounter with an NPC inspired by Tom Cruise's character Vincent from the 2004 film Collateral. Vincent takes a cab driver hostage and forces him to drive across Los Angeles to take out five assassination targets in a single night. Unlike the film, Jason doesn't have to drive this gun-toting guy around all night, but he does sound conspicuously Cruise-like.

Red Dead 2 isn't the only entry in Rockstar's back catalog to make a cameo in GTA 6. In addition to a dedicated episode all about the main story of GTA 5, there are plenty of references in Rockstar's latest to previous installments of its marquee series, especially on the radio. In an episode of the podcast "Fuck, Marry, Murder," the two hosts discuss the many murders of Eddie Low, a serial killer who appears in GTA 4 and GTA 5.

Fans of deeply upsetting horror films, it's time to live out your worst nightmares. If you explore or swim around Hyde Island as Jason or Lucia, you'll potentially trigger an ambush. You'll be kidnapped and knocked out, temporarily lose all your items, and discover your captor has put a Saw-style detonation device on your neck. You'll awaken in a storage container while a voice speaks over a TV set. After an ominous countdown, you'll be hunted in an arena by a man with night-vision goggles, a sniper rifle, and a ferocious dog. You'll need to sneak around in the darkness to gather as much ammo as possible to take the hunter down, get your stuff back, and escape the island.

An optional side mission in Gullet Marsh includes a reference to one of the most memorable video game memes of all time, as Jason is abruptly attacked by a "giant enemy crab." You can read more about this deep cut here, which was inspired by E3 2006 and has been referenced in countless video games since.
