#3450. ‘Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall’ Review: PTA’s Spellbinding Concert Doc Is a Gorgeously Tender Performance

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on October 2, 2026 during the 2026 New York Film Festival. Janus Film will release the film in limited theaters on Friday, November 20.]

Paul Thomas Anderson‘s eye for vivifying music onscreen dates back to the late 1990s when, after “Boogie Nights,” he made Technicolor mini-masterpiece music videos with his ex-girlfriend Fiona Apple — or made a San Fernando Valley-sized shrine to Aimee Mann with his third feature, “Magnolia.” Since then, he’s kicked around with HAIM while turning one third of its Los Angelino triumvirate, Alana Haim, into a screen actress. He’s shot for Radiohead and made a regular collaboration with band member Jonny Greenwood to create some of the 21st century’s most memorable scores. Many young cinephiles now associate the mischievously lilty notes of “Phantom Thread” with the poison promise of new love and obsessive creation. Related Stories If There’s Generative AI in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ It’s Not the First Time David Fincher’s Used It Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage

Last December, PTA teamed up with Geese frontman Cameron Winter to film, while operating his own Panavision camera, his solo stage performance at Carnegie Hall, running through sparse piano arrangements of tracks off his solo album, “Heavy Metal.” The result, a 72-minute film now being distributed roadshow-style by Janus Films before inevitably living on the Criterion Collection, is a stunning arrangement of its own: a deeply achey, sincere but never cloyingly earnest concert movie that’s tender to the point of frailty. (Benny Safdie counts as a co-producer, and the film’s scratchy New York quality and setting can’t help but have his imprint.)

The matted-hair, lithe Winter can seem a bit uncomfortable in his own skin in the public eye, as he did onstage ahead of “Cameron Winter at Carnegie” at its New York Film Festival world premiere at Alice Tully Hall. But on the piano, laser-beamed into his songcraft, he’s quietly electrified, at seemingly at peace as his tenorous vocal glissando and nimble fingerwork on the piano produce shiveringly tender folk ballads that echo Harry Nilsson and Van Morrison. (The usual comparisons to Tom Waits and Rufus Wainright are right, too, but Winter is his own strange thing.) If you weren’t previously sold on the wily Winter antic rock chaos of Geese — rapidly becoming one of the most popular contemporary art rock bands of these times — you’re about to. Paul Thomas Anderson has created a rhapsodic shrine to the man that is nonetheless ballad-sized in its emotional scale.

Winter, in December, played and sang to a sold-out crowd of more than 2,700 at the stately cultural temple that is Carnegie Hall, and this film can at times feel like a religious experience, an incantation, a lonely vigil. The singer/songwriter was 23 at the time of the performance, one year older than Bob Dylan when he headlined Carnegie Hall, and similarly at the precipice of major fame. Fixed on a mobile rig that will at times careen and whoosh across the stage when not otherwise holding on Winter, Anderson’s camera catches the expressionism and chiaroscuro of stage lights illuminating and fading off the singer’s face.

The result is hynoptic, a concert film up there with “Stop Making Sense” but for introverts. Songs like the popular single “$0” acquire an even more wrenchingly somber quality as a lovelorn protagonist rues being exploited by a relationship (“You’re making me feel like a dollar in your hand / You’re making me feel like I’m a zero dollar man”). Stripped of production, his indie hit “Love Takes Miles” plays even better. While many of the songs sort of hover in the same key and bleed into one another, that makes for an all the more transfixing experience. The lack of an interstitial anything save for a sweet prologue and moving coda make for experience also that’s immersive, deep, and the kind whose truth you can feel somewhere in your body even if you can’t quite articulate it.

#3448. GTA 6's T-shirts Are True Works of Art

Please let me purchase that Rusty Anchor wet T-shirt contest prize

We've known for some time that fashion would be a big deal in Grand Theft Auto 6. In Rockstar's official promotional materials for the game, both Jason and Lucia were prominently featured wearing stylish clothing, from Lucia's body-hugging gold dress to Jason's slick Miami Vice-inspired aqua sport coat. Even supporting characters like Brian wear Tommy Bahama-inspired aloha shirts yanked straight from the closet of a dapper middle-aged stoner. GTA 6 has drawn praise from all quarters for its scrupulous attention to detail in every aspect of the game, and there's one area the developer went far, far harder than it needed to: the vast and immaculate selection of T-shirts.

Having a diverse wardrobe isn't just a fun little customization touch in GTA 6. If you're reported for committing a crime in Leonida — and this will happen very often — police will be able to recognize you based on your car, your physical appearance, and what you're wearing. Keeping a couple spare outfits in your trunk or hastily buying a new ensemble on the run can be the difference between a successful job and ending up busted (or wasted).

I'm taking my time with GTA 6 and still kicking around the introductory area of Key Lento. I know I should be putting money in my family savings account. It would probably be in my best interest to learn how to drive without sideswiping semi-trucks or taking out stop signs. Perhaps I ought to be buying more guns. Instead, I'm trawling South Leonida for all the vintage and souvenir shops I can find. You can keep your fancy cars. I've got a T-shirt collection to maintain.

Much like in real life, you never know when you're going to find a gem in a vintage boutique or souvenir shop in GTA 6. My prized Rusty Anchor shirt came from an optional mission where you take Cal for drinks, he has a few too many, and you have to take him home. Apparently Cal won a wet T-shirt contest at the Anchor and this was his reward, but he's too hungover to claim the prize.

During my wanderings, I also discovered a riff on that three-wolves-howling-at-the-moon shirt that everyone had about a decade ago, including me. But this one has gators on it. I bought it from Sharleen's yard sale in Jason's very own neighborhood of Key Lento. She had a couple of inexpensive clothing items on offer, including some pretty slick teal sneakers that were clearly inspired by Air Force One low-tops. I was delighted to learn that there are multiple yard sales in the game, including one in Port Gellhorn where you can buy a dupe of Arthur Morgan's hat from Red Dead Redemption 2.

Even the cheesiest souvenir shops, like Leroy's in Key Lento, have the exact kind of "so bad it's good" T-shirts you'll see dozens of times over the course of a weekend in a tourist trap. Do I need to spend $38 of my ill-gotten dollars on a horrendous blue granny shirt with a dolphin on it, with "Vice Beach" written in collegiate font? Certainly not. But I am tempted.

Rockstar has a bunch of GTA 6 merch on its official website, including T-shirts, though much of it is currently sold out. Here's hoping they expand the offering with a couple of these in-game gems. If you're hard up for a three gator moon shirt though, you can already find them on Amazon and Etsy.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Sharon Horgan had a string of British hits (including a couple we'll talk about here), before scoring stated successes with Divorce, Shining Vale, and Bad Sisters. She's quickly rising in the ranks of TV super-producers, the acerbically funny HBO Max rom-com Youth (in which she also stars) being just the latest.

This earlier series created by and starring Sharon Horgan is a family sitcom that feels far more believable than most, seeing Irish primary school teacher Sharon (Horgan) hooking up with American ad exec Rob (Rob Delaney) over the course of a week, only to discover that she's pregnant once he returns home. They don't really have feelings for each other, but decide to give it a go at being a couple, eventually falling into marriage just before the birth of their child. There are lots of jokes and plenty of acerbic dialogue, but this isn't Married... with Children. Sharon and Rob can be a bit nasty to each other and to their sloppy friend group, but there's also something rather sweet in the show's conviction that having someone to be a mess with can be one of life's great joys. Stream Catastrophe on Prime Video.

A little more of a high-concept here, but nevertheless an effective show about reimagining yourself in middle age. Younger follows Liza Miller (Sutton Foster), a recently divorced woman in her 40s who finds that age is a barrier to reentering the publishing industry she left years earlier. After a compliment convinces her that she could pass for a younger woman (poor thing), she manages to convince the right people that she's just 26 in order to land an entry-level job. Seven seasons of misadventures ensue, but much of the show revolves around the twisty-turny relationship between Liza and Josh (Nico Tortorella), a tattoo artist in his twenties. Stream Younger on Netflix.

Bridget Everett stars as Sam Miller, who struggles to find her new direction after moving back to her hometown to care for her dying sister. (Don't worry: There's plenty of comedy in the drama, and it's not as heavy as it sounds.) She's solidly middle-aged and starting over, kinda—making new friends in a familiar environment where she has to confront the past and the future alike. Luckily, her love of singing—and a community of goofy oddballs—are there to help. It's another story of a person of a certain age, trying to rebuild their life following an upheaval. Stream Somebody Somewhere on HBO Max.

When all else fails: Start a punk band. This drama from Sally Wainwright (Gentleman Jack) sees five women start a punk band as a lark, just a fun way to kill some time by entering a local talent context. The women realize very quickly, though, that they're very, very pissed off—about the workplace for women, menopause, a diminished dating pool, caring for aging parents and grown children—all of it tied up in the ways in which we treat women, and particularly middle-aged women. The band is a way to reclaim their voices, which doesn't erase or negate any of their problems nor drama (and there's plenty here), but gives them a platform with which to make some noise about it. Stream Riot Women on Britbox.

More of a traditional sitcom, not that there's anything wrong with that, this one builds a lot of goodwill with the performance of Leanne Morgan, its lead and co-creator (alongside Susan McMartin and Chuck Lorre). She plays the show's lead: a Knoxville, Tennessee wife and mom, who finds herself suddenly single in her 50s after her husband of 33 years leaves her. It's a genial, old-school hang-out show with a phenomenal veteran supporting cast that includes Kristen Johnston, Ryan Stiles, and Tim Daly. Stream Leanne on Netflix.

Michele Buteau, who also co-created the series) stars here as a fashion-forward stylist who'd devoted herself to the wrong guy for way too long. As the series opens, Mavis Beaumont is ready for a fresh start, putting herself and her career first—which does not preclude falling into a number of romantic entanglements. As she says more than once, she's going to take on the fashion world with a "body-positive attitude, cute v-neck, and some lip-gloss." Stream Survival of the Thickest on Netflix.

Certainly the goofiest take here on the idea of starting over in mid-life, this is very much a traditional three-camera sitcom, albeit one with a stacked cast of TV legends. Writer Melanie (Valerie Bertinelli), beautician Joy (Jane Leeves), and soap diva Victoria (Wendie Malick) wind up spending a wild night in Cleveland after a plane to Paris is diverted, discovering in the process that, while they're seen as over-the-hill back in Los Angeles, they're all Ohio 10s—though the sassy caretaker of their house, Elka (Betty White), might not agree. Stream Hot in Cleveland on Paramount+.

She'a s hair younger than Alex, but Fleabag (she's only ever referred to as "Fleabag") is trying to rebuild her life after a bad breakup, with extremely mixed results. This very dark comedy-drama follows a free-spirited, deeply angry single young woman living in London and sharing her romantic ups and downs via confessional asides to us, the audience. She falls, rather reluctantly, for "The Priest" (Andrew Scott)—while she's a confirmed atheist, and he's obviously not, the show doesn't turn aside from the general messiness of the situation. Phoebe Waller-Bridge won separate Emmys as the star, creator, and writer of the series. Stream Fleabag on Prime Video.

Maisel was one of Prime’s first truly buzzy original series, a comedy-drama from Amy Sherman-Palladino (Gilmore Girls) about the title’s Midge Maisel (Rachel Brosnahan), a long-time New York housewife of the late 1950s who discovers a talent for stand-up comedy. Inspired by the real-life careers of comedians like Totie Fields and Joan Rivers, the show is warm and welcoming, with great performances and dialogue; it also achieves something rare in being a show about comedy that’s actually funny. Stream The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel on Prime Video.

The big life change in this earlier Sharon Horgan hit is a little different: Julia Johnstone's mother had been a big help in taking care of Julia's children, but she's not going to do it anymore, leaving this working mom (Anna Maxwell Martin) to take the full brunt of childcare for the first time (her husband in the picture, but not much use). She joins up with other working moms involved with a local support group, including shallow Amanda (Lucy Punch), star of her own ongoing spin-off. Stream Motherland on Prime Video and Britbox.

#3446. 11 2000s Sitcoms That Have Aged Like Fine Wine

2000-2010 was a transformative decade for sitcoms, bridging the gap between traditional multi-camera comedies and the more experimental, character-driven shows that would define the 2010s. While network hits like Friends and Everybody Loves Raymond carried over their ratings dominance from the '90s into the early 2000s, a new generation of sitcoms challenged the genre's established conventions.

Throughout the decade, sitcoms increasingly embraced unconventional storytelling, surreal humor, and more complicated protagonists. Shows like The Office and Curb Your Enthusiasm helped popularize mockumentary techniques and cringe comedy. Other sitcoms experimented with serialized storytelling, genre-blending, and narrative structures that rewarded attentive viewers. These innovations helped lay the groundwork for the increasingly ambitious sitcoms of the 2010s.

The 2000s also produced some remarkably prescient social satire. Comedy could explore cultural anxieties that would only become more relevant with time. Corporate greed, celebrity obsession, technological advancement, and changing social expectations provided fertile ground for comedies whose observations now feel surprisingly contemporary.

However, the most successful sitcoms of the 2000s haven’t always aged well, like Two and a Half Men. Meanwhile, DVD box sets and reruns allowed audiences to discover overlooked comedies, while shows that struggled during their original runs developed cult followings and earned critical reevaluation. Some even received unexpected revivals years after their cancellations.

Ultimately, the 2000s sitcoms that have aged like fine wine weren’t necessarily considered the biggest, funniest, or even the best during their original run. Some were timeless from the beginning, while others were so far ahead of their time that audiences are only now fully appreciating them.

Scrubs was beloved during its original run, but its blend of surrealist comedy and emotional realism has become even more distinctive. While J.D.'s elaborate daydreams provided absurdist humor, Scrubs embraced truly sad episodes, never shying away from the grief, burnout, and moral dilemmas that come with working in a life-or-death profession.

More importantly, it recognized that humor wasn't a distraction from those experiences, but a necessary coping mechanism for healthcare workers. That understanding has helped the show remain perennially popular, leading to the 2026 Scrubs revival that feels like a natural continuation rather than an exercise in nostalgia.

The Bernie Mac Show was ahead of its time in its refreshingly unconventional portrayal of Black family life. Rather than depicting an idealized father figure, Bernie Mac played an impatient, frequently overwhelmed guardian who reluctantly takes in his sister's three children.

Breaking the fourth wall to address the audience directly, the show explores resentment, discipline, and the sacrifices of raising children. This feels particularly relevant as contemporary family comedies increasingly embrace imperfect caregivers and nontraditional households. Its use of direct-to-camera confessionals and uncomfortable family truths also anticipated the mockumentary storytelling that would become a sitcom staple later in the years to come.

My Name Is Earl has only gotten better with age, especially in its refreshingly optimistic approach to redemption and accountability. At a time when television increasingly embraced morally bankrupt antiheroes, Earl Hickey was something of an anti-antihero: a petty criminal determined to become a better person by making amends for his past mistakes.

Rather than mocking its working-class characters for their shortcomings, the sitcom treated them with genuine empathy, recognizing that even deeply flawed people are capable of change. Its emphasis on personal responsibility, forgiveness, and second chances feels especially refreshing in an era of increasingly polarized moral judgments.

My Name Is Earl’s unresolved cliffhanger ending remains a bitter aftertaste. However, the show's underlying philosophy has aged beautifully.

Girlfriends was groundbreaking during its original run, but its portrayal of Black female friendship has only become more significant with time. Following four women as they navigate careers, relationships, and personal growth in Los Angeles, the sitcom challenged the limited roles available to Black women on television without reducing its characters to stereotypes.

More than two decades later, Girlfriends feels like a precursor to shows such as Insecure, particularly in its exploration of professional ambition, sexual independence, and complicated female friendships. Its frank discussions of Black womanhood also remain strikingly relevant, demonstrating how many of the social pressures its characters confronted have persisted long after Girlfriends' series finale.

Arrested Development is the definitive example of a sitcom that found a larger audience after its cancellation. The comedy struggled with ratings during its run, only to become a cult phenomenon through DVD sales and streaming. Arrested Development reshaped American sitcoms — its densely layered jokes, elaborate callbacks, unreliable narration, and interconnected storylines were practically designed for binge-watching.

Beyond its innovative storytelling, Arrested Development's satire of a wealthy, self-absorbed family whose privilege repeatedly shields them from consequences feels increasingly relevant. Two decades later, the Bluth family's entitlement and spectacular incompetence have only become satirically sharper with time.

Aliens in America was arguably a decade ahead of its time, tackling Islamophobia, xenophobia, and cultural prejudice through the unlikely premise of a teenage sitcom. Premiering in 2007, the short-lived comedy followed Raja, a Pakistani Muslim exchange student who moves in with a Wisconsin family expecting someone else entirely.

Rather than making Raja the punchline, Aliens in America frequently turned its humor toward the ignorance and prejudices of his American hosts, challenging stereotypes while remaining genuinely funny. At a time when hit dramas like 24 routinely associated Muslim characters with terrorism, Aliens in America pushed back against American ignorance and Islamophobia.

Winning three consecutive Outstanding Comedy Emmys, 30 Rock was a masterpiece but never a mainstream ratings juggernaut. When the sitcom entered its final season in 2012, it had roughly one-third the audience of The Big Bang Theory.

However, its cultural footprint has grown considerably. The comedy's rapid-fire jokes, obscure pop culture references, background gags, and elaborate callbacks reward repeat viewing, making 30 Rock particularly well-suited to the streaming era.

Discover how these beloved '90s sitcoms have stood the test of time, with our ranked list of the best classic TV shows that have aged like fine wine.

Meanwhile, its relentless satire of media consolidation, celebrity branding, and corporate interference in entertainment has become increasingly prescient. What was once an industry-insider comedy now feels like a remarkably accurate portrait of modern Hollywood.

Peep Show has created an enduring cultural legacy through its painfully relatable portrayal of social anxiety and arrested adulthood. Following two dysfunctional roommates perpetually struggling to be adults, Peep Show is an anti-sitcom that took cringe comedy to uncomfortable new heights.

Its innovative first-person camerawork and internal monologues exposed the disconnect between its characters' outward behavior and private thoughts, trapping viewers inside the insecurities and selfish impulses behind their humiliating decisions. This psychological realism anticipated the painfully self-aware humor of shows like Fleabag.

More than two decades after its premiere, Peep Show's examination of social awkwardness, self-sabotage, and the inability to get one's life together feels more relevant than ever. Like a bold red wine, it might make you pucker at first, but those with a sophisticated palate will appreciate its complexity.

The Boondocks is an animated sitcom whose biting satire of American society feels just as relevant two decades after its premiere. Following brothers Huey and Riley Freeman as they navigate life in a predominantly white suburb, the Adult Swim comedy fearlessly tackles racism, politics, consumerism, and celebrity worship.

Rather than limiting its criticism to white America, The Boondocks also challenged contradictions within Black popular culture, particularly the glorification of violence, materialism, and fame. Its episodes satirizing sensationalist media coverage, celebrity scandals, and the commercialization of Black identity often feel almost prophetic.

Set within the morally bankrupt corporation Veridian Dynamics, Better Off Ted satirized corporate greed, unethical innovation, and the prioritization of profits over people. Nothing better illustrates how far ahead of its time the show was than its infamous “Racial Sensitivity” episode, where the company devises increasingly ridiculous workarounds rather than fixing the technology that can’t recognize Black employees.

What seemed like absurdist satire in 2009 now feels like a remarkably accurate critique of corporate irresponsibility and reliance on flawed technology. ABC canceled Better Off Ted after two seasons, but there was plenty of juice left. Underappreciated during its original run, Better Off Ted is one of the best obscure sitcoms that everyone should watch.

#3445. What ‘Digger’ Has in Common with Gary Oldman’s Winston Churchill and Charlize Theron’s Megyn Kelly

Tom Cruise‘s performance in Alejandro González Iñárritu‘s “Digger” is one of the boldest and most entertaining of the actor’s career, as he suppresses not only his usual movie star charisma but his entire way of walking and talking to play paunchy, aging oil tycoon Digger Rockwell. Cruise is barely recognizable in the role, which is about as far from heroic characters like Pete “Maverick” Mitchell and Ethan Hunt as Cruise’s Ron Kovic in “Born on the Fourth of July” was from race car driver Cole Trickle almost 40 years ago.

To aid in his complete transformation, Cruise called on one of the best prosthetic designers in the business, Kazu Hiro. Hiro has turned Gary Oldman into Winston Churchill (“The Darkest Hour”), Charlize Theron into Megyn Kelly (“Bombshell”), and Dwayne Johnson into “Smashing Machine” Mark Kerr, but transforming Cruise into Texas oilman Digger Rockwell was a whole new task — one made even more challenging by Iñárritu and Cruise’s persistent striving for perfectionism, and constant eagerness to try new approaches. Related Stories If There’s Generative AI in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ It’s Not the First Time David Fincher’s Used It Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage

“Alejandro is an amazing director, and he has lots of ideas,” Hiro told IndieWire. “Every day he comes in with a new idea, and we have to come up with an answer for how to achieve it. And Tom is really professional, and expects everybody else to be at that same level, ready for any situation. After the first day of testing, I learned that I had to stay flexible to respond to whatever they wanted.”

To that end, Hiro created modular prosthetics whose parts could easily be swapped out and moved around, so that Cruise and Iñárritu could constantly try new looks. “Sometimes with heavy makeup, you can’t change it,” Hiro said. “I created prosthetics that could be mixed, so we could make new designs on the spot — try this forehead with these cheeks and this nose, then change it.” Creating Cruise’s look was a constantly evolving process throughout the long prep period. “We didn’t have a clear answer until the end of rehearsal.”

Hiro’s mandate at the beginning was a bit open-ended, which gave him room for artistic exploration but also made it difficult to zero in on a precise look. “Alejandro said the character was 76 years old and an oil tycoon,” Hiro said. “He also said he didn’t want the character to look like Tom, but he still wanted to see Tom in the character.” To try to find a concrete image for Digger Rockwell, Hiro immersed himself in research.

“I researched real oil tycoons and how they aged and what kinds of lifestyles they had,” Hiro said. “Those lifestyles affect how they age.” As Hiro did more and more research, however, he realized that there was no one look that defined the entire profession he was trying to represent. “Everybody looked so different, so in the end I relied more on the storyline and how this particular character behaved.” The idea, in keeping with the slightly heightened style of the film as a whole, was to exaggerate Cruise’s features but keep the character realistic.

Hiro began with a 3D scan and life cast of Cruise, which he used to sculpt his designs. His paramount concern was allowing the actor to be as expressive as possible under the makeup. “The important part is to make the prosthetic very soft so he can move,” Hiro said, noting that three weeks before shooting, Iñárritu called with a significant change. “He decided that Digger should be 65, not 76, so I quickly made a new design. Tom is around that age, but he looks much younger than a normal 65. Under his eye was exposed and the rest of the face was covered, but I made it thin to give him freedom.”

In addition to Digger’s face, Hiro was also tasked with creating an upper body for an early scene in which Cruise would be seen stripped down to his pajama pants. The body prosthetic was intended only for that one scene, with a lighter bodysuit created for the rest of the movie. “We made a light version of the padding for under the costume, because we don’t need to see the skin after that first scene,” Hiro said. “For the first scene we made a silicone prosthetic that was a lot heavier — the body padding was around 10 pounds, but the silicone was 40 or 50.”

During one of Cruise’s costume fittings, he told Hiro he wanted to feel the weight of the silicone throughout production. “He tried the body prosthetic on and said, ‘I like this, I want to wear it every day,'” Hiro said. “I told him it would be really heavy and hot, but he said he was training and would be fine.” Since gluing the body prosthetic on every day would be extremely time-consuming, Hiro created a strong spandex foundation and glued the prosthetic to it so Cruise could slip it on each day.

“He wore that for the whole film,” Hiro said. “One time he said, ‘This is so heavy, it’s really hard on my back.’ I thought, ‘Okay, you asked for it,’ but he went through with it and finished the film, so that was amazing.”

#3444. You Can Try WhatsApp's New Disappearing Text Messages Early

Like Snapchat messages, WhatsApp's "View Once" feature is a great way to send things you don't want living on your friends' devices. You can send voice messages, photos, and videos that will "self-destruct" after they're opened, limiting (if not eliminating) the risk of your friends keeping them forever. However, View Once has a major limitation: While WhatsApp will let you send voice memos and images that way, you can't use it to send texts, meaning every one you send will live on (unless you unsend it yourself).

That's now changing. As reported by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp is now beta testing View Once for text messages, too. Soon enough, you'll be able to send voice memos, photos, videos, and texts as one-time-only messages. That way, you can send sensitive information via text—say, a password or an important account number—without worrying about it persisting. Here's how it works: You craft your text message as you usually do, but rather than tap the send button, you hold it. You'll see the usual "Schedule message" option, but once the feature rolls out, you'll also find a new "View Once" option as well.

As mentioned above, this feature is currently in testing, so it's only available to WhatsApp beta testers. What's more, only the Android version of the beta has access at the moment, so iOS beta testers are out of luck. (That said, the WhatsApp iOS beta is perpetually full, so there's not much you could do even if WhatsApp made this test available on iPhone.)

If you have an Android device, you can enroll in the WhatsApp beta to try out "View Once" text messages today. According to WABetaInfo, the feature is live as of WhatsApp version 2.26.45.6. To enroll, open the WhatsApp beta page on the Google Play store and enroll your account in the beta. If you don't have WhatsApp on your phone already, download it here; if you do, reload the page and install the latest update. This will update your existing WhatsApp app to the latest beta version.

#3442. I Tested Pangram to See If It Can Really Detect AI-Generated Content Like It Claims

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

We know it can be difficult for human beings to spot AI-generated content, but can detection software fare any better? Pangram is one of the leaders in the field, promising a "near-zero false positive rate" by looking at "subtle cues" in the writing, based on a training and feedback model comparing human-made content with the AI equivalent.

You'll find arguments on both sides of the debate as to whether or not Pangram's claims stand up. After a short story was flagged by Pangram and then judged to be free from AI, the detection engine has been accused of bias against text from minority writers.

Proponents of Pangram would point to an ongoing reward offer—currently at $3,950—available to anyone who can find a pre-2019 (and pre-LLM) piece of writing that Pangram falsely flags as being AI-written. So far, the reward is unclaimed.

As the AI detector has recently added AI image and video detection to its capabilities, it seemed a good time to put Pangram's analysis skills to the test for myself. Here's how it performed in the three different content types.

On the human side, I picked out 10 of my most recent articles for Lifehacker, known to be written by a person because I personally wrote them—in the traditional way, I fretted over word choices, went back and changed sentences, and accidentally left in a variety of typos that editors thankfully fixed.

For the AI content, I rotated between ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude, and got the LLMs to write 10 articles with the same headlines and the same approximate number of words, for a tech-savvy audience. I even asked the AI apps to vary their language use, so that the output would "read less like an LLM has written it."

Pangram's AI text detector lets you upload files, but to make the task a little harder, I copied and pasted all of the text into the online article, so it wouldn't be able to rely on any metadata included in the file. The scans got the correct result each and every time: Human-written text came back as 100% human, and AI-written text came back as 100% AI.

What's more, Pangram was certain about its results. All of the human writing was marked as highly likely to be human, and the vast majority of the AI writing was marked as highly likely to have come from an LLM. There were only a handful of phrases or sentences across thousands of AI words that got a "medium" rather than a "high" ranking for AI.

Now, there have been some edge cases where Pangram has got it wrong—like a poem repeating the same six words thousands of times—but as far as this sample goes, it can't be faulted. Clearly, my writing is too idiosyncratic and too clunky to be confused for the smooth sheen of AI-produced prose.

To be fair, I do have another advantage over AI: I can actually test out devices and apps in a way that LLM bots can't. ChatGPT can't experiment with One UI 9 (at least not yet), though it can scrape the web for various experiments and tests that real people have done.

However, I was able to fool Pangram to some extent by alternating AI paragraphs with human-written paragraphs. The text was flagged as AI, but the percentage estimate was typically lower (20-25%) than what it actually was (around 50%). If you're offloading some but not all of your writing to AI, some of it might slip though as real.

Image and video detection is the new string to Pangram's bow, so I sifted through my phone's photo and video library for some pieces of content to test the AI on. Again, I used copy and paste to get the files into Pangram rather than uploading them, to limit how much information the AI detector could get from metadata.

Again, all the human-made content was recognized as such, with a very high level of certainty—whether it was complicated crowd shots or simpler images of natural scenes. Presumably, there are even more signals to go off than there are with writing, including camera movements, colors, style, consistency, and composition.

Next up, I generated a few images and videos in Google Gemini and ChatGPT, requesting results that would look as photorealistic and "non-AI" as possible—the resulting files covered people, animals, and buildings. As before, I used copy, paste, and a few screengrabs to try and limit the metadata Pangram had access to.

Here, too, the AI identification was spot on, with all of the artificial content recognized as such, to a high level of confidence. This is perhaps not surprising: I think AI images and especially AI video still have more "tells" than AI writing, especially if you've seen a lot of it, so I wasn't expecting Pangram to fail here.

I did try experimenting with real photos that had a little bit of AI in them, what with tools like Gemini and ChatGPT now so good at image editing, as well as creating pictures from scratch. These were marked as "unsure" by Pangram, though to cut it some slack, only a small amount of the images were altered.

As with the text, the best way to beat Pangram's detection systems seems to be to include some AI embedded in human-made content. It will most likely still fail the "100% human" test, but the tests I ran showed that Pangram is less certain in these cases, or underestimates the amount of AI there actually is.

Increase the level of AI, and the detection gets more reliable—but if you're only using AI for a small part of whatever it is you're making, it's less worthwhile using AI tools anyway. As far as these tests go, Pangram's claims about accuracy check out, making it a useful tool if you need to ensure something is AI-free.

#3441. Sorry, Vice City, but You’re the Most Boring Part of GTA 6

When Grand Theft Auto 6 was first announced, fans were thrilled at the prospect of returning to Vice City. The Miami-inspired location has always been one of the series’ most memorable locations, its neon-lit streets standing in contrast to the grittiness of Liberty City. While I was as excited as anyone to go clubbing and spend some time on the beach, after 70 hours, GTA 6 has struck me with one surprise thought: Vice City is the least interesting part of Leonida.

I don’t mean to say that Vice City sucks — far from it! It’s an immaculately designed video game city with more environmental diversity in any given corner than some open-world games fit into an entire map. The fact that it’s one of my least favorite places to spend time is more a testament to every other location in GTA 6’s Florida-inspired world. From small towns to the deep wilderness, every corner of Leonida is a delight to discover because every area feels so different.

I blame GTA 6’s opening chapter for spoiling me rotten. Jason and Lucia’s story begins in the Leonida Keys, a brilliantly constructed introductory area that I fell in love with instantly. As someone who is fascinated by the Florida Keys, the real islands that the location is based on, I was thrilled to find a digital space that so accurately captured a genuinely surreal part of America. The real Keys feel like an isolated nation, densely packing stores and suburbs onto narrow islands. The Leonida Keys feel both like an idyllic vacation hideaway and a mundane suburb, which gives GTA 6’s opening chapter such a distinct feel from the rest of the game. The small town nature of it makes for one of my favorite chunks of any GTA game.

Even after getting out of the Leonida Keys, it’s still a while before you get to Vice City. First, Jason and Lucia spend a stint upstate hopping around some small towns separated by vast farmland. Port Gellhorn has the feel of an industrial town, the kind of place that’s lined with used car lots. Some great action set pieces come out of that setup; one time I busted up a well-guarded abandoned bowling alley and wound up in a gritty gang shootout.

Way south of there, you’ll find Capri, another highlight. The squeaky-clean upper-class town is full of boutique clothing stores and high-end cafes. When Jason and Lucia arrive there, they are immediately profiled by street cops who clock them as poor outsiders who don’t belong in town. It stings considering how hard up for cash the two are when they get there, which turns the town itself into one of GTA 6’s greatest antagonists. Screw this place!

Even the stretches of map that seem empty at a glance are fascinating. Some of my favorite moments so far have been spent in Lummox County, which is largely made up of woods and mountains (despite IRL Florida not technically having those). Some of the best date spots and activities are up there, hidden alongside hiking trails. It’s also home to some true weirdos, like a group of “conservationist” gun nuts who say they are controlling the ecosystem by shooting at invasive lizards. Those weirdo discoveries make what could have been a dull, empty area into a place that I keep feeling compelled to bike around.

Between all of those areas, there are so many little pockets of the map to love. Hullet Marsh hides one of the game’s weirdest secrets amid the alligators. Tiny islands like Belpoint are quaint little escapes worth seeking out. Even unassuming stretches of road, like the area under Buckskin Swamp, will lead you to decaying mini-golf courses that make you feel like you’re in a state with a lot of history to it. I’ve seen every corner of the map, and very little of it has felt like a waste of exploration.

Vice City is excellent too, of course. It’s a perfect representation of Miami, right down to the hotel pools that I’ve sat by while visiting my brother, who lives there. Vice Beach is a highlight, and the various Keys around the city give the area a lot of diversity. It’s more just that I expected all of that. I know that Rockstar can get the hustle and bustle of cities right, because I’ve been playing GTA games since I was a kid. It’s more exciting to see GTA 6 branch out into more intimate towns and figure out how to make those just as exciting without the sports cars and nightclubs. GTA games have explored these spaces before, but the sheer mass of them here helps Leonida feel like a fully realized state with its own economic and political nuances from region to region.

My relationship to Vice City as it stands is similar to the relationship I have to Manhattan as a Brooklynite. It’s work island. Clock in, make some money, and leave the city limits at sunset to actually live a little. I’ll remember my mini-golf games more than the hours I spent sitting in traffic on Vice City’s freeways.

GTA 6 takes some liberties with its world around Vice City

#3440. House Of The Dragon: Caraxes Icons Officially Announced For 2027

House of the Dragon has been a fascinating experiment for the longevity of George RR Martin's wider universe in television form, and for the most part, it has been largely successful. Though the series has lost a bit of momentum as it wore on, and it never reached the lofty heights of the original Game of Thrones, it has done enough to show there's plenty of potential moving forward in new stories.

Having said all of that, the most important thing that it did was restore faith after a horrendous Season 8, which really could have seen the franchise as a whole die on the spot. If you do count yourself among the many fans of House of the Dragon, there's a new release that celebrates one of its coolest winged beasts, Caraxes.

Over on the Iron Studios website, the manufacturer of physical memorabilia has confirmed that pre-orders are now open for Caraxes - House of the Dragon - Icons, a new highly-detailed polystone rendition of Daemon's dragon. The figure clocks in at 14" (H) x 10.9" (W) x 13.3" (D), making it the perfect size for display area at home, without taking up too much space.

The official description for the statue reads as follows:

"Inspired by the acclaimed HBO series House of the Dragon, Caraxes joins the Icons line from Iron Studios. Known as the Blood Wyrm, Caraxes is one of the most fearsome dragons in the world of Westeros and serves as the mount of Daemon Targaryen.

"This collectible faithfully recreates the dragon's distinctive appearance, featuring his elongated neck, powerful wings, menacing expression, and unique serpentine physique. The detailed sculpt captures the creature's imposing presence, while the themed display base enhances the dramatic presentation inspired by the Targaryen legacy. Expertly crafted and hand-painted, this statue is a must-have for fans of the series and collectors of fantasy-themed collectibles."

If you aren't familiar with Caraxes' story, he's widely known as the Blood Wyrm thanks to his blood-red scales, serpentine build, and immense ferocity. First claimed by Prince Aemon Targaryen, he spent many years without a rider after his death before being claimed by Daemon, and playing a crucial role throughout the events of House of the Dragon.

By the time of the events of Game of Thrones, some 170 to 200 years later, dragons are seemingly entirely a thing of the past, until Daenerys hatches her three eggs and rules the skies (until she doesn't).

As mentioned earlier, the statue is currently available for pre-order, with an expected release date of April—June 2027. It's also worth noting that the images included in the listing are of the current design, which is still awaiting approval from the licensor. It's also not cheap, coming in at a considerable $399.99, though in this case you are paying for the quality.

As for the final season of House of the Dragon, there's a bit of a wait for that as well, with the final season not expected to debut until 2028 (though we don't have anything more specific than that just yet).

Taking place about 172 years before the events of Game of Thrones, House of the Dragon tells the tale of the rise of the Targaryens, the only family of dragonlords to survive the Doom of Valyria.

#3439. The UK and some other countries don’t get more Siri AI usage with iCloud+

Apple this week revealed the additional Siri AI usage you’ll get if you have an iCloud+ subscription. This ranges from doubled limits for a 200GB plan to 20 times for a 12TB plan.

However, the company’s support document reveals that some countries will not get access to these increased usage allowances …

Apple hasn’t yet specified the standard limits applicable to Siri AI usage, instead saying that these will vary depending on anything from the feature used to the overall level of demand at the time. However, it did list the proportional increases you get with paid iCloud plans.

However, tucked away in the small print in the company’s support document are some exclusions. One of them is no surprise: EU countries.

Siri AI isn’t available at all in the EU due to Apple’s perception of potential antitrust issues. Essentially, Apple believes that if it launches Siri AI there, it will be required to give competing AI services the same level of access to its devices. But three other countries are specifically excluded:

Apple gives no explanation, simply saying:

Increased access to Siri AI with iCloud+ is subject to Siri AI availability and is not available in Brazil, the EU, UK, or South Korea.

However, I have a strong suspicion about the reason.

What all three countries have in common is that they’ve taken a strong antitrust stance with Apple on a number of occasions over a range of issues.

It may be that Apple has genuine concerns about how regulators might respond if they effectively throw in free access to increased Siri AI usage. The company may fear that this would be viewed as anti-competitive by implicitly disadvantaging other AI services.

A less charitable take would be that Apple is firing a warning shot across the bows of these countries, seeking to communicate that there are consequences for what it views as attacks on its ecosystem. If customers are angered by missing out, Apple might be hoping that these feelings would be directed at regulators rather than the iPhone maker.

What’s your take? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

#3438. How a Filipino Facial Expression in ‘Forgotten Island’ Became a Universal Symbol of Representation

As soon as the first clips from DreamWorks’ latest animated film, “Forgotten Island,” started popping up online, there was one specific shot that caught on fire online — the lip pointing. It happens at a goodbye party for Raissa Molina (Liza Soberano), who is heading to Caltech. Her best friend Jo (H.E.R.) is late to the party and asks around to see where Raissa is, when an older woman points with her lips in the right direction. It’s a small moment, a visual gag that can easily go over the audience’s heads amidst all the other jokes in the sequence. But audiences familiar with Filipino culture immediately caught on to it, as did Latino fans and many others who recognize that gesture as the most potent and accurate way to point at something. Related Stories If There’s Generative AI in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ It’s Not the First Time David Fincher’s Used It Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage

“That moment had been in the script since the first draft, because we wanted to put in as much as we can from our personal experience with Filipino culture,” director Joel Crawford told IndieWire. “Growing up around Filipinos, the lip point was something that was so specific and unique to me, so it’s beautiful that it transcends into other cultures. Adding that felt like a celebration of it, but also something that makes characters feel real. And in adding that specificity about the culture, it ends up being the most universal aspect of the movie because it invites everyone in.”

The lip pointing may not happen in a pivotal scene, or be important for a character, but it became a sort of symbol for the film’s approach to representation. Later in the film, Jo does the lip pointing because an animator thought it would be a good idea to reprise it, after learning about its place in the culture. Indeed, in addition to having an authentically Filipino cast and a cultural consultant to really capture Filipino culture, the animation team found their own ways of homaging or capturing aspects of Filipino culture to bring to the movie.

When creating the character of Jo, the animation team based a lot of her hand expressions on Filipino skater Margie Didal and her own hand gestures, while the villainous Manananggal’s movements were created by the animation team watching choreography done by Filipino-American dancer Phil Tayag, who brought a pop locking influence to the vampire-like creature.

“When we first approached DreamWorks and Universal with this story, it was important to everybody that we got every detail of this story and this culture right,” director Januel Mercado said. “

After challenging what was thought possible with DreamWorks animated films in “Puss in Boots: The Last Wish,” Crawford and Mercado push the studio’s visuals forward with “Forgotten Island.” With most of the story taking place on the island of Nakali, which is populated by all sorts of mythical creatures, to really capture the fantastical possibilities of this world, the movie’s visuals go wild, taking inspiration from 1990s Filipino art as well as anime from that time period.

For Crawford, the big lesson learned from “The Last Wish” was that you could take big swings in the animation style and the visuals, but you could also do specific things in the story with those visuals. Indeed, when it came to “Forgotten Island,” the idea of memories and friendship became not only central to the story of Jo and Raissa, but also to the eclectic visual styles represented in the movie.

“The idea became that we could push the animation styles to represent the different ways people recall memories,” Crawford explained. “We didn’t need to be limited by Western CG-style animation, but actually bring in some of our own nostalgia into it and make sure it fit the characters. When Raww tries to explain what happened when he met Jo and Raissa, he sees himself as way cooler than he is, so he sees himself as Goku or Guile from ‘Street Fighter,’ the animation going 2D in an action-heavy tone. But when we meet Mermahn, he is very shallow and narcissistic, and we felt his glamorous point of view fit the aesthetic of ‘Sailor Moon’ with the silly kind of heart-shaped lens flare.”

Still, just because you can go Super Saiyan doesn’t mean you let go of reality. Instead, the directors worked with the head of cinematography, Scott Cullen, to make sure the film had a live-action look to it. The idea was to capture the nostalgia of growing up, while being able to feel the camera in the space the action takes place in, as if it was a physical set.

“Joel and I really wanted to make sure you feel like live-action, you feel the cameras there, and the way the light interacts with the lens is reminiscent of tangible photos we grew up taking, where you don’t know how they’ll develop,” Mercado said. “ We wanted to add imperfections, and to have interaction of weather on the camera, like condensation of rain and droplets on the camera.”

This all added to making “Forgotten Island” look like a part of the evolution of DreamWorks Animation, while standing out as something entirely fresh and unique. As Crawford said, the studio doesn’t really have a specific house style like other big studios. “Every movie requires innovation and pushing boundaries and finding solutions,” he added.

#3437. Eight Hacks Every Tidal User Should Know

I recently switched from Apple Music to Tidal, and I'm happy I made the change. The main reason is AI-made music: Tidal has stricter AI filtering than any other major streamer. The second reason is audio quality. While all major music streaming services do basically the same thing, Tidal's focus has always been on streaming music at the highest possible quality. While other streaming services have more or less "caught up" in terms of pure sonic fidelity, Tidal still is better at getting that quality to your speakers, if you know a few tricks.

If you're switching from Apple Music or Spotify to Tidal, you probably want to bring your playlists with you. Tidal points new users toward third-party transfer tools like TuneMyMusic and Soundizz. They both have a free tier, but they only transfers a few hundred songs gratis. My playlists are way bigger than that. The easy solution is to grumble and sign up for a month, then cancel when your tracks are transferred, but that didn't sit well with me. A playlist is just a collection of song names, so why should I have to pay anything to transfer it? To solve the problem, I came up with a simple script that transfers playlists from Apple Music and Spotify to Tidal. I will not be charging a fee. Here's how it works:

Download your playlist as a .txt file. You can do this directly from Apple Music under File>Library>Export Playlist. You can't from Spotify, but the free site Exportify will download any of your playlists as a spreadsheet file you can save.

Install Python on your system. Double click "install certificates" in the folder that opens after installation.

Download this script. Save it in the same file as your playlist.

Run the script: (For Mac, open Terminal. For Windows, go to the Command prompt. Type python3 on a Mac or py on Windows.) Drag the script into the terminal window and press enter. It should ask you to drag your downloaded playlist into the window next.

Sign in to Tidal. Hit "Approve" to give permission for Tidal to run the script.

Have a banana. The script is going to search for all the songs on your playlist and match them to Tidal's library, so it can take a little while. I tested it with a playlist from Apple Music with 2,397 songs. It took about 20 minutes and found 2,362 of my tracks, a 99% success rate.

Fix the leftovers: The program creates two separate text files for "orphans." One is songs it couldn't find and one is songs it might be worth double-checking manually.

If everything goes well, your large playlist should be available on Tidal.

Note: The script uses a community-created library to talk to Tidal, so it could stop working if Tidal changes things up.

Like most streaming services, Tidal has a "heart" button called "add to my collection." You can click on any track, album, or playlist to "like" and saved it. But Tidal also has a separate, somewhat mysterious "Save for Later" option that puts songs, albums, and playlists into a separate collection. There are a couple reasons for this. First, it keeps a running list of new-to-you music waiting for you on a rainy day, and secondly, it (presumably) affects your recommendation algorithm differently. While Tidal isn't open about every detail of its recommendation algorithm, I assume "save for later" has less weight (if any) on your future recommendations than "add to my collection."

On Tidal, tracks that are 100% AI-generated get an "AI" badge, earn no royalties, and are never placed on a Tidal-curated playlist. Users can flip a switch in Settings to either allow or disallow AI content, too. Simple, but there's a bit of nuance that goes beyond the on/off switch. You have to set the AI-toggle separately on each device you use Tidal on, even if it's the same account. I guess this is so I can listen to AI music in my car but not at my desk? Sadly, AI detection is not a science, so some AI-made, and partly AI-made, tracks may still get through.

If you're streaming music from a music app through Bluetooth, the output is automatically compressed to a lower quality, and your phone stays in charge, so a phone call or a notification can interrupt your music. But Tidal's Tidal Connect feature skips the middleman. Music streams directly from your wifi to your speaker and your phone becomes a remote control, so you can take a call, go for a walk, and even run out of phone battery and the music will keep playing.

Have an external device with Tidal Connect compatibility.

Make sure your speaker or other output device and phone or computer are on the same wifi network.

Click the icon again to switch back to your phone.

Plenty of wifi speakers don’t support Tidal Connect, so check before you buy. Tidal keeps the full list of supported devices on its site. There's everything there from WiiM Mini—a $99 small box that adds Tidal Connect to speakers you already own—to dCS components that cost more than a car.

Tidal Connect isn't the only way to get the highest quality audio from Tidal. You can go for an old school, wired path like I have. I play audio from my desktop and route it directly to a mixer via USB. Here's the set-up:

Settings > Streaming > Audio Quality: Max.

Sound Output: choose your mixer as the output device instead of your computer’s speakers.

Exclusive Mode: On. It’s under Sound Output > More Settings. Tidal sends audio straight to the mixer at each track’s native sample rate, without your computer resampling it or mixing in system sounds.

Force Volume. It's in the desktop app next to Exclusive Mode, under Settings > Streaming > Sound Output > More Settings. Force Volume means Tidal will always output at the highest volume. You'll be controlling the actual volume from your mixer.

To check what your mixer can handle, look at its maximum sample rate:

Mac: Open Audio MIDI Setup (in Applications > Utilities), click your mixer, and open the Format menu. The highest number listed is your ceiling.

Windows: Go to Settings > System > Sound, click your mixer, and look under Output settings > Format.

My cheap-ass mixer tops out a 16-bit/48kHz which is CD quality, but not Tidal's top of 24-bit/192kHz, but at least I can control the EQ. Speaking of...

It's much cooler to turn dials than mess with computer settings. Tidal doesn’t have an equalizer, so if you’re using Tidal Connect or a wired connection, you'll need something to shape the sound. Here are some options:

Your computer: System-wide EQ apps, like Equalizer APO on Windows or SoundSource on Mac, can adjust Tidal’s output. They don’t work with Tidal Connect though, which bypasses your computer’s audio processing.

Your speaker’s app: If you use a Tidal Connect speaker or streamer, it probably has a companion app for EQ.

A mixer or audio interface: Channel EQ knobs let you adjust bass, mids, and treble by hand, in real time.

Your speakers: Many powered speakers and studio monitors have low and high controls on the back.

A stereo receiver or amp: Old-school bass and treble knobs still work in 2026.

Most of Tidal's catalog streams as "better-than-CD quality" FLAC files at every subscription tier, so you might be inclined to click "play music at highest quality on everything." but settings are only as good as the gear you're using, and there are times when lower quality is the right choice. Here's when to turn down the settings:

When you're in your car: CarPlay and Bluetooth cut audio down to CD quality or less before it reaches your speaker, and with road noises, it usually doesn't matter anyway, so turn the streaming down to "High" instead of "Max." Or download your playlist before you leave, if you must have "as good as possible" audio.

You have a data cap and are off wifi. Top quality audio requires huge file transfer, so set your mobile data to High or Low and save Max for wifi.

Your connection is spotty: To avoid buffering, a lower setting keeps the music playing.

This isn't a universal hack, but some Android phones have microSD card slots, which can save you a lot of hassle if you're downloading a lot of audio files—an album at high quality might top 1GB, so having an external source will save you a ton of hassle. If your phone has a microSD card slot, go to Tidal's settings, find "download destination" and choose the memory card.

#3436. 25 Years Later, Dragon Quest’s Island-Hopping Epic Gets Better in Every Port

The Dragon Quest franchise has been around for longer than some of us have been alive, and its first entry in 1986 was one of the JRPG genre’s pioneers. Over the years, the launch of a new title in the series has been a big deal, especially in Japan. Before players missed work to play Grand Theft Auto 6, they were using sick days to topple wicked dragonlords.

In North America, Dragon Warrior 7 (the last entry in the series to bear that localized title), arrived after two previous installments weren’t released outside Japan. Interest had waned. When the game hit stores on Nov. 1, 2001, it was as difficult to find as its NES predecessors had been. And when loyal fans finally tracked it down, we wound up being disappointed. But over the years, Square Enix has made some adjustments and tried again on multiple occasions. Happily, each new release of Dragon Quest 7 gets better than the one before it.

Dragon Quest 7 spent a long time in development and arrived late enough in the original PlayStation’s life cycle that it felt decidedly old-fashioned by the time any of us got the chance to play it. The visuals were a step above anything the Super Nintendo offered, finally rendered in 3D with a camera that players could rotate. But the experience still felt a bit like a step back compared to the flatter but more detailed environments of late PS1-era games like Final Fantasy 9. In some respects, it was a relic from a time many players had moved on from.

The quest’s opening hours didn’t correct that first impression. I remember playing for three hours without encountering a single enemy mob, which just felt odd. In the typical Dragon Quest game from years prior, you could head outside the castle walls within a few short minutes. An hour into the adventure, you would have already battled dozens or even hundreds of monsters and leveled up your characters several times. Instead, I had to spend that time solving tedious puzzles.

Slow opening hours eventually gave way to a lengthy quest with plenty of appeal, but I didn’t actually stick around to experience those later events until Dragon Quest 7: Fragments of the Forgotten Past launched on the 3DS on Sep. 16, 2016 in the West. Despite making its debut on portable hardware, the new release offered a superior way to experience the adventure.

The single change I appreciated most was an update to the formerly tedious first few hours of play. The introductory dungeon, with all of its levers and backtracking, was gone. Introductory areas still ate up more time than I was accustomed to, but they fit within a single gaming session and left me with time — and enthusiasm — to progress to more interesting activities.

The 3DS version offered other enhancements, as well. The bottom screen provided a helpful glow when the player approached stone tablet shards, a major component of progression. Players had a lot less guesswork to find essential items, a smart adjustment that eliminated a lot of pointless frustration.

Another new feature recapped the story, in case players stepped away for a few days, weeks, or longer. Accessible from the pause menu, a chronological log listed every major event that had occurred, along with hints about where to go next. (Later games in the series, all the way up to Dragon Quest 11, would keep this addition.) While exploring, party members might also offer suggestions if consulted, sparing players from some of the ambiguity that had been a franchise staple since its first installment.

Quality-of-life enhancements didn’t stop there, either. The game also introduced enemy mobs players could see in the field as they explored. Leveling up required less grinding, and menus were modified and streamlined. A map on the bottom screen made it easy to spot nearby points of interest. Most importantly, players could make a quick save outside of churches if they needed to stop playing suddenly. For a portable game, that option was a must.

Dragon Quest 7 on the 3DS remained the best way to play the game for a decade, until Dragon Quest 7 Reimagined launched in February 2026. Available on Switch, Switch 2, PlayStation 5, Windows PC, and Xbox Series X, the updated take on the classic adventure introduced a breathtaking new art style. Presented like a diorama, the gorgeous visuals paired nicely with quality voice acting to bring the world’s story to life like never before.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

The newest release also introduced new changes to the character vocation system, allowing party members to adopt two vocations at once and gain mastery in both of them. Changing a class no longer required a time-consuming visit to Alltrades Abbey, either. And on the world map, striking weaker monsters defeated them automatically with lesser rewards, a welcome compromise that eliminated the need to endure tedious skirmishes. There were other changes, as well, including multiple difficulty presets, a shared inventory, and auto-revive after battle for party members who perished in the fight.

For RPG fans in 2026, these were smart adjustments. Few players appreciate busy work and random encounters that slow the pace more than necessary. It’s good to see developers revisiting past triumphs and modernizing them for contemporary audiences to enjoy. If at first you don’t succeed, try, try again. It certainly worked for Dragon Quest 7.

#3435. How to Transfer Your Playlists to Tidal Music for Free

I recently switched music streamers from Apple Music to Tidal. I like Tidal's strict anti-AI features, the fact that it pays higher royalties to artists than other major streamers, and its focus on high quality audio. I wrote a post featuring eight hacks for Tidal users, but I wanted to highlight one in particular: How to transfer playlists without paying anything.

Tidal points new users toward third-party transfer tools like TuneMyMusic and Soundizz, which are both easy to use, but they're subscription services, and they only transfer a few hundred tracks for free. I have thousands of tracks, saved in a ton of playlists. The easy solution was to grumble and sign up for a month, then cancel when the tracks were transferred, but it just didn't sit well with me. A playlist is just a collection of song names, so why should I have to pay anything to transfer it? To solve the problem, I came up with a simple script that transfers playlists from Apple Music, Spotify, and any other service that lets you download your tracks as a text file to Tidal. I will not be charging a fee.

Download your playlist as a .txt file. You can do this directly from Apple Music under File>Library>Export Playlist. You can't from Spotify, but the free site Exportify will download any of your playlists as a spreadsheet file you can save.

Install Python on your system. Double click "install certificates" in the folder that opens after installation.

Download this script. Save it in the same file as your playlist.

Run the script: (For Mac, open Terminal. For Windows, go to the Command prompt. Type python3 on a Mac or py on Windows.) Drag the script into the terminal window and press enter. It should ask you to drag your downloaded playlist into the window next.

Sign in to Tidal. Hit "Approve" to give permission for Tidal to run the script.

Have a banana. The script is going to search for all the songs on your playlist and match them to Tidal's library, so it can take a little while. I tested it with a playlist from Apple Music with 2,397 songs. It took about 20 minutes and found 2,362 of my tracks, a 99% success rate.

Fix the leftovers: The program creates two separate text files for "orphans." One is songs it couldn't find and one is songs it might be worth double-checking manually.

If everything goes well, your large playlist should be available on Tidal.

Note: The script uses a community-created library to talk to Tidal, so it could stop working if Tidal changes things up.

#3434. Curry Barker Would Have Completely Reshot ‘Obsession’ If He Could

It’s been quite a year for Curry Barker. In September 2025, he brought his $700,000 horror film to the Toronto International Film Festival, where it sparked a bidding war that Focus Features won for $17 million. That hefty price tag turned into the deal of the century, as “Obsession” went on to become a half-billion-dollar box-office sensation, with audiences growing week to week. It was clear the then 26-year-old “YouTuber” (a moniker Barker rightfully dismisses) was something special. This was not just a flash in the pan, but a real talent with a seemingly boundless number of ideas and movies he wanted to make. His next film, “Anything but Ghosts,” was already in the can by the “Obsession” premiere, a yet-to-be-announced third film is in the works, while potential franchises (“Texas Chainsaw Massacre” and “Obsession,” Barker sees the One Wish Willow story device having “Knives Out” anthology-like potential) linger in the background. Related Stories Director Brian Duffield Had to Find a New Form of Visual Storytelling for ‘Whalefall’ How ‘Paper Tiger’ Evolved When Jeremy Strong and Anne Hathaway Couldn’t Reprise Their ‘Armageddon Time’ Roles

Which is why it’s interesting that Hollywood’s hottest new director took time out from editing (he’s cutting “Ghosts” himself) and writing (“I have my next thing that I’m working on — I’m really excited about it, and nobody knows anything about it, which is super exciting”), and an unexpected Oscar campaign (“Obsession” is a legit contender for Best Picture, Actress, and Original Screenplay nominations), to make a 5-minute short film, “Mama Bear.” On this week’s episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Barker talked about how the success of “Obsession” interrupted his established flow of churning out short-form content for his popular YouTube channel.

“I have two or three short films where I’m like, ‘Oh man, this all took off really quickly, and I have this short film idea I’ve been dying to do,” said Barker on Toolkit. “I actually have no time to do those short films, and then justifying if it be would be worth my time to do them when I need to be writing this, I need to be editing this, and I need to be doing press for this.”

It’s less about Barker’s desire to scratch the itch of the shorts he never got to make, but more about a hesitancy to step away completely from the iterative process by which he learned his craft — justifying the brief time he took off to make “Mama Bear” because he felt the need to sketch.

“It’s fun to have that playground because the features are bigger stakes,” said Barker. “We were like, ‘Okay, this is a short film: We can do weird stuff. Let’s come up with crazy rules that don’t make sense, and experiment.’”

Barker and his “Mama Bear” cinematographer — his young brother Riley, who worked on the “Obsession” camera department — created different rules for the camera, as Curry is still trying to hone his discipline for storytelling within longer takes. Not only would they shoot a narrow 4:3 aspect ratio, but the Barker brothers denied themselves the ability to move the camera left, right, up, down, or dolly in.

“I do have a lot to learn,” said Barker of making “Mama Bear.” “It’s so funny because I was having dinner and I told someone, ‘Oh, I’d love to shadow on Ari Aster’s set.’ And someone was like, ‘Well, you’re Curry Barker, what are you going to shadow for?’”

His 2026 meteoric rise has allowed Barker to collect a group of more experienced peers he views as mentors — including Aster, Bill Hader, Zach Cregger, and Rian Johnson — and successful producers, like Jason Blum, investing in his career, but he believes there’s a misconception of what comes along with “making it.”

“People think that once you’re in this club, you’re in the club, and everyone talks to everyone. But no — you’re in a bubble, and I want to know how Zach Cregger writes his outline. I want to watch him do it,” said Barker. “You’re all alone. Your process is your own, and you figure this stuff out on your own. Once you get into this league, there’s no one telling you, ‘Well, actually you do it like this, this, and this.’ It’s whatever you learned all along your journey; that’s your process.”

One of the most impressive things about the self-taught Barker’s journey is how quickly he turned himself into a successful actor/writer/director/editor. In 2018, when Barker left Alabama to come to Los Angeles to pursue a career in movies, he saw himself as an actor. Despite all the story scenarios dancing around his head, the idea that he would become a screenwriter was laughable.

“I never would’ve thought I was a screenwriter. I didn’t make great grades. I made Cs and Ds, and I wasn’t the best in English class,” said Barker, who naively assumed professional writers were the kids who won spelling bees: “I just thought to be respected as a writer you have to be that.” Barker credits taking screenwriter Aaron Sorkin’s MasterClass as what opened his eyes. “It was the first time I thought, ‘I can do this, too.’ It’s really just about being creative and cracking a story, and there are rules, there’s structure.”

Directing organically grew out of Barker pulling together collaborators to shoot sketches and shorts for him to act in. Barker, half-joking, likes to say he realized one day that what he was doing was directing, and that he both enjoyed “telling people what to do” and had a knack for it.

What Barker accomplishes in a single shot — establishing a tonal balance that teeters between horror and comedy, combining blocking and camera movement to edit within the frame — is remarkably sophisticated. But Barker, who studies and strives for what masters like Kiyoshi Kurosawa can accomplish, quickly says he fell short in “Obsession.”

“Things that you might think we pulled off [with longer takes in ‘Obsession’], we reshot,” said Barker, who on the podcast described in detail a key early scene between Bear (Michael Johnston) and Nikki (Inde Navarrette) in the bedroom that had to be reshot because the action took too long to unfold. “I think Ari [Aster] said once that if you realize you needed to give this information in four seconds, but then it took 25 seconds, you’re stuck with 25 seconds.”

Curry Barker, the editor, is Curry Barker, the director’s harshest critic, giving him a bird’s-eye view of what he believes is the director’s inability to envision the required pacing of how a scene will play on screen, even if it might feel unnaturally fast on set.

“Every single oner that I’ve shot in my career has been a problem in the edit,” said Barker. “I think there’s two ways to fail at something. You can either fail, realize that it didn’t work, get scared of it, and then be like, ‘Well, in my last film I did a bunch of oners and then it killed me in the edit, so I’m not going to do that anymore.’ Or you can fail, realize how you did it wrong, and try to get better at that for the next time.”

As Barker discussed at the Future of Filmmaking Summit last month, that iterative process is key to how he got where he is, and it’s a mindset he clearly hasn’t given up. When asked how “Obsession” would have been different if he had more money, Barker doesn’t talk about locations, sets, special or visual effects, or scenes he envisioned that he couldn’t pull off — in terms of scale, he likes both writing and directing within set limitations.

“I would’ve reshot everything,” Barker answered without hesitation. “If I was finishing the edit before we got into TIFF, and you were like, ‘Dude, this is really good, we really love this movie, we think it has potential, but we want to give you $10 million to reshoot the whole thing, I would be like, ‘Deal.’ I would take it.”

“I think it’s so funny to look back and think about that now,” Barker catches himself, knowing he’s talking about a film that broke the box office and catapulted his career. “Now I wouldn’t change anything because I would be too scared to touch it.”
