#3433. GTA 6: Should You Kill Or Spare The Skunk Ape In "Advanced Skunk Apenomics"

One of the various Strangers & Freaks side quests in Grand Theft Auto 6 deals with the legendary Skunk Ape, an elusive sort of Bigfoot-esque creature that's stalking around the swamps in Pelican Valley. Early on, you'll be able to trigger a quest by viewing the signs posted around the starting area and contacting Kirk, eventually tracking down a series of effigies in the swamp.

!!! WARNING: THIS GUIDE HAS SPOILERS FOR THE SKUNK APE MISSION IN GTA 6 !!!After you've found each of these effigies and waited a few days, Kirk will get in contact with you for a meetup in the swamps again, this time with a partner and a helicopter. Jason will have to shoot the Swamp Ape, aka Mr. Mangrove, with a tranquilizer gun from the helicopter, which will cause the creature to run into a shed and collapse. Once Jason tries to pick it up, some very strange things happen.

First, players will turn into a frog and be required to hop around the docks and eat several flies, and then will be transferred into a fly and be asked to find Kirk, listening in on the Swamp Ape hunter's nefarious plans to use the QR code tattooed on Mr. Mangrove for a large sum of money. When Jason wakes back up, you'll have to choose whether to save Kirk from the Swamp Ape.

Killing Mr. Mangrove the Skunk Ape is the most straightforward option of the bunch, and has the clearest and most immediate reward. First, if you're planning to kill the Swamp Ape, be sure to question Kirk about who Harry Sherrick is by both threatening and questioning him. You'll have found out by now that Kirk was planning on leaving you for dead anyway, so putting a little fear into him isn't all that big of a deal.

Afterward, you can kill Mr. Mangrove and choose to save Kirk. This will result in a monetary reward of anywhere between $10,000 and $12,500 depending on if you questioned/threatened Kirk, and he'll then promise to give you a cut of the QR code payout, but that doesn't end up happening, seeing as the helicopter will explode and Kirk and Noah will die.

There are actually two different ways to spare the Skunk Ape in this mission, the first being to shoot Kirk with the rifle, which will knock him unconscious. The Skunk Ape will then pick him up and carry him off into the swamp. The second option is to just let the Skunk Ape go ham on Kirk and squeeze his head until it pops. Mr. Mangrove will then carry Kirk's corpse off into the swamp as well.

Seeing as Mr. Mangrove will still be alive, it's very likely he can be found later in the game or even after you've completed the main story and return to Leonida for the Post-Game experience. As of this writing, it isn't clear specifically what this entails, but based on my experience with another Strangers & Freaks mission involving the mutant form of Kyle, there are likely benefits to leaving the Swamp Ape alive.

If sparing Mr. Mangrove is anything like the Hulk-Kyle "Buddy?" quest, my guess is that the Swamp Ape will clear out the Kingfisher drug dens in the swamp area, though this has yet to be confirmed.

Despite not knowing the exact benefits of sparing Mr. Mangrove, it's likely that all the Strangers & Freaks missions have benefits that are immediately clear. While the $12,000 or so seems like a good chunk of change, assuming Mr. Mangrove helps clear out the Kingfisher operations, you'll be able to go into these encampments with zero resistance and arguably benefit more than you would from the cash.

That said, this is only really worth it if you're completing the mission in Chapter 2, as going back to these areas when you're in the later chapters isn't all that much of a challenge anymore. Further, since I haven't been able to confirm the specific results of the Skunk Ape surviving and taking Kirk into the swamp, it'd be understandable if you want to take the cash reward instead.

It's also entirely possible that you can find the Skunk Ape in the endgame and claim the QR code prize that Kirk and Noah were after, though this is purely speculation as of this writing. This GTA 6 guide will be updated as soon as more details become available.

#3432. Banks, FAA, Microsoft, Apple – no systemic attack on the US, says White House

A set of major tech outages in close succession is leading some to speculate that they are connected, and that the US is under systemic attack by a hostile state.

All the evidence suggests otherwise, with individual explanations for each of them – and the White House is now saying as much in a bid to put fears to rest …

Whether there was or wasn't a cyber attack, I wouldn't believe a single word from the White House.

On Thursday, a widespread Microsoft 365 outage ran into the following day when two unrelated issues coincided. Friday saw a nationwide ground stop of US air traffic due to a communication issue affecting all air traffic control centers. On Monday, a bug in a Chase bank system saw disruption not only to the bank itself, but also other banks where Chase was a party to a transaction. Finally, yesterday saw many Apple services offline, with retail stores also affected.

The Apple outage doesn’t appear to have been significant enough to have reached the administration’s radar, but CBS News reports secretary of state Marco Rubio saying the others are unrelated.

“The Microsoft incident has nothing to do with what we saw with the FAA. The FAA has nothing to do with what we saw with the banks a few days ago. These issues that we’ve seen from a technical standpoint are completely unrelated one from another,” Rubio said […]

“We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind. Each of them are distinct, and they’re different in their causation.”

The statement was backed by Senator Mark Warner.

Democratic Sen. Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, also said on Tuesday that there’s no indication these incidents are the result of an attack.

Warner went on to say that the ability of AI systems to find vulnerabilities at “unprecedented speed” does, however, mean companies and government agencies alike need to be ready to patch vulnerabilities immediately.

#3431. Eight Important Router Settings You Should Check (or Change)

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Your router is a key piece of your home network, as it connects all of your other devices to the internet. This also makes it a highly valuable target for attackers and can leave your data vulnerable—especially if you simply plug your router in with its default settings unchanged. Whether your router is brand new or it's been a while since you audited your existing setup, these are the key settings to check and change right now.

Your router's security protocol determines how encryption and authentication work to protect data that's transmitted over your network. WPA3 Personal is the newest standard and the most secure, so if it's available on your router, enable it. It's compatible with devices that support Wi-Fi 6. Some older devices may not work with WPA3, in which case the WPA2/WPA3 Transitional mixed mode is a good alternative. At minimum, set your router to WPA2 Personal (AES).

Some routers ship with factory default login credentials, which are the username and password you need to access your device's admin dashboard. (This is not the same as your network name or wifi password, which you set up later.) Default router passwords are searchable online, which leaves your router's admin settings open to anyone. Once you get into your dashboard for the first time, change the default credentials and enable two-factor authentication for your admin account if available.

While some newer routers do have unique, device-specific defaults, it's a good idea to check this setting and ensure it's secure. If you're prompted to create custom admin credentials during the setup process, do it.

Your network name, or SSID, is how your network appears when you search for available wifi. By default, this may be the name of the router brand or a short string of characters, but you should choose something unique to your network. Make sure there's no identifying personal information, such as your name or house number. While you may be tempted to hide your network and obscure your SSID, this may actually make your information less secure, so keep this setting disabled. You can, however, add "_nomap" to the end of your network name, which prevents your router's physical coordinates from being mapped by location databases.

The password to access your network should also be unique and secure and should not include obvious personal information. One option to keep it memorable and easy to type is to create a passphrase using five to seven unrelated words that, combined, have at least 16 characters.

Being able to log into your router's admin dashboard from anywhere may be useful if you have complex networking needs or troubleshooting issues that often have to be addressed when you're away from home, but it also leaves an entry point open for attackers. Turn off remote management to prevent anyone from accessing your dashboard unless they are on your network. (This is also a great reason to have strong, unique admin credentials.)

Two additional settings that leave your network vulnerable are Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS) and Universal Plug and Play (UPnP). The former lets users connect to your network with a PIN, which can be vulnerable to brute-force attacks. The latter allows smart devices to easily connect to your network—but this also allows malware to spread more readily. You may need to have UPnP on in order to connect devices initially but should disable it afterward.

Any easy win for your network security is segmenting traffic to different networks, so if one is compromised, the data on the others remain unaffected. Many wifi routers have a "guest mode," which creates a separate SSID and password that you can share with visitors instead of giving them your primary network credentials. You can also set up a separate network for all of your smart home and IoT devices so exploitable vulnerabilities in these devices don't put your computers, phones, and other connected devices at risk too.

Routers run a type of software—called firmware—just like any other device. Firmware controls the router's core functions and is not immune to vulnerabilities, which can be exploited by bad actors. And, just like other types of software, manufacturers occasionally push updates to patch these flaws. Check your router's dashboard to see if automatic updates are toggled on. Some devices require an opt-in for auto updates during setup, so you should enable them if they are off. Some routers may even require manual updates—in this case, set a monthly or quarterly (at minimum) calendar reminder to check for patches.

#3430. How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’

[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. MUBI will release “Minotaur” in theaters on Friday, November 20.]

World-class Russian filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev (“Leviathan”) returned to the Croisette this year in Cannes competition with “Minotaur,” having recovered from a near-fatal illness. After contracting a severe case of COVID in 2021, he reacted badly to the Sputnik vaccine and was put into a medically induced coma for 14 days. When he came out of it, his arms and legs were paralyzed due to Guillain-Barré Syndrome. He lay flat on his back for a year.

When he left the hospital in Germany in 2022, as he told me while at Cannes this year, he was in a wheelchair. While he says he hasn’t watched TV for 20 years now, “I watched a lot of films online,” he said through an interpreter on the roof of the Palais. “I read some things. I did not know if I would ever be able to walk again, to live again as a normal person. I have still now some consequences. I’m not at my best. I have regained completely the motion of my hands, but I have still a bit of a difficulty walking.” Related Stories If There’s Generative AI in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ It’s Not the First Time David Fincher’s Used It Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage

But he did manage to shoot his sixth feature film last year, but not in Russia. After nine months of waiting, in the spring of 2023, he let go of one expensive project (“Jupiter”) for which he couldn’t seem to raise funding. “I said, ‘Let’s put it on ice, we’ll come back to it later. I don’t want to sit and wait for years and years for you to find the money. I want to make a film now.'”

So instead the filmmaker focused on a parallel project he had also been developing, an adaptation of Claude Chabrol’s 1969 thriller “The Unfaithful Wife,” starring Stéphane Audran as a well-heeled wife cheating on her husband, which was later remade as “Unfaithful” with Richard Gere and Diane Lane. The result, “Minotaur,” is the “Leviathan” Oscar nominee’s first film in nearly a decade, since 2017’s “Loveless.”

At the same time that the filmmaker was coping with his illness, four years ago, at the start of the Ukraine war, he made the decision to leave Russia and move to Paris. Going home would mean the risk of being considered a traitor or an enemy of the state in Russia. “It might result in us becoming what is called foreign agents; it’s a hard thing,” he said. “Maybe this will happen, maybe not. Let’s not be too pessimistic, but mostly all independent journalists are saying that their oppressions are going to get even harsher, and that I think we have decades ahead of us before things get better.”

His 16-year-old had been studying at a French high school in Moscow before the war. “His French was pretty good,” said Zvyagintsev. “So it was an obvious choice. And also, my wife [has been] in love with France for a long time, she has been learning French for many years. So it was a choice, also for both of them, and for their future.”

How’s his French? “Zero,” he said. “The other reason for me was that France is the homeland to cinema; that’s where cinema was born, and also there are so many cinephiles among spectators. Also here in France, directors have the final cut. In the states, it’s much harder to get in a position where you are not censored; it’s not a producer or someone who decides instead of you.”

The filmmaker set about creating believable Russian locations in Riga, Latvia, which still resembles its neighbor country. “The dormitory suburbs around Riga look exactly like Russian dormitory suburbs,” said Zvyagintsev. “A Russian eye would not be able to distinguish between Russia and Latvia in this instance. As for interiors, Anton’s flat was constructed as a set, so it’s a constructed set, and the villa where the main characters live is a contemporary building, a very modern one, and you could find something exactly like this anywhere.”

When it came to finding his cast, the casting director put out a call for Russian characters of a certain age. “Every actor from anywhere who is interested in working with you, they will send you a video presentation,” said Zvyagintsev. “They can be from Argentina, London, Moscow, Paris, wherever. You send them a scene they have to play, and they make a self-tape for you on their iPhone. Before, I despised self-tapes, but it’s convenient, because now with everybody scattered around the world, it’s the only way for us to work. We could not possibly pay for all the people I wanted to check to come to Riga to make a real-life casting. There were people also from Riga who do speak Russian.”

One serious issue for Russian actors still living in Russia was the possible repercussions of participating in a Zvyagintsev project. “I would talk to them about the script and show them parts of the script, so that they know what they’re getting involved in, because, of course, they were at risk of getting blacklisted,” he said. “Most of them, with heartache, refused to take part in the film, but there was one who accepted, and I’m still completely amazed at his courage. It’s the main part, the main character, [actor] Dmitriy Mazurov. I said to him, ‘Are you sure you want to film with me?’ And he said, ‘If I’m not doing this part, I don’t know what I’m doing in acting.'”

Of course, the filmmaker took a different approach to the Chabrol story. “In the first minute, the story is completely revealed,” he said. “We understand that she is being unfaithful, so then all the film is about observing him, observing her, trying to understand, hesitating, and trying to guess what is going on, and while he observes, the spectator starts doing it along with him. And after the murder, actually, he goes back to this position where he’s mostly observing her reaction to the disappearance of a lover, yeah, and she knows what’s going on, and again it’s about observation.”

The filmmaker loved one bravura sequence that is 20 minutes long without any dialogue at all. “The sequence after the murder, it’s 20 minutes, even a little bit more, with not one subtitle, so you only observe his actions, and there are no words: it’s extremely cinematic in its essence.”

And Zvyagintsev added many telling details from the real world, from corruption to the war. “The Chabrol film is much more classical,” he said. “It follows a pattern: he killed, then he’s discovered, and then he will be punished. And I wanted to break up this classical structure and to invent something different based on our Russian realities.”

Was shooting the movie a physical challenge? “When you are full of inspiration, when you are searching constantly for solutions, the light, the sets, the performance of the actors, you don’t feel fatigued in the same way,” he said. “There is such a joy in making the film that is, in your head, real. I think it’s the best drug there is.”

Next up, he will try and resuscitate “Jupiter.” ” I have met some producers who are interested in it,” he said, “so hopefully we will be able to get it moving again.”

#3429. MacPaw’s Moonlock comes to iPhone, helping users detect potential scams

After launching Moonlock for Mac last year, MacPaw is bringing its scam-detection app to iPhone today. Here are the details.

When MacPaw launched Moonlock on the Mac, the company described its new app as something that “complements Apple’s built-in security tools, protects from Mac-specific malware, and helps you understand cybersecurity better.”

In practice, the Mac app includes real-time protection against potential threats. Users can also manually scan their Mac for malware, including suspicious files hidden in system folders and email attachments.

Beyond that, Moonlock includes a VPN to encrypt internet traffic, a network inspector that shows where apps are sending data and lets users block connections to specific countries, and an AI-powered scam detector that analyzes messages pasted into the app for signs of phishing. It also helps users review and adjust macOS security settings.

Today, MacPaw is launching Moonlock for iPhone, a move the company says “helps people recognize potential scams, understand their iPhone’s security and take practical steps to improve it.”

Unlike the Mac version, Moonlock for iPhone doesn’t scan for malware, as iOS prevents third-party apps from accessing other apps and their files. Instead, it focuses on identifying potential scams, checking for exposed personal information, and helping users improve their iPhone’s security.

On the iPhone, Moonlock lets users quickly check suspicious texts, screenshots, and QR codes for phishing, in addition to checking whether their email addresses have appeared in known data breaches.

As MacPaw explains it, Moonlock’s Scam Detect “helps people check suspicious messages they encounter throughout the day. Whether it’s a text message, a screenshot shared by a friend, or a QR code, users can paste, scan or share content directly with Moonlock and receive an assessment explaining why something may be suspicious.”

Here’s Oleg Stukalenko, Head of Product Management at Moonlock by MacPaw, on today’s launch:

“When we launched Moonlock, our goal was to make cybersecurity something anyone could understand and use. But so much of what people do today, from banking to everyday conversations, happens on their phones. Bringing Moonlock to iPhone felt like the natural next step. We want to help people spot a scam before they tap, see where their security stands, and know exactly what to do next.”

MacPaw’s Moonlock for iPhone is free to download, with subscriptions available for $9.99 per month or $49.99 per year.

#3428. The iPhone Duo Is Getting Face Unlock

Apple dropped iOS 27.2.1 last week, patching a handful of security vulnerabilities and bugs—including two iMessage flaws that let people read messages they shouldn't. But while most of us are running this version (or should install it as soon as possible), others are running something different—iOS 27.3.

Apple is currently beta testing the third major update in the iOS 27 era, and anyone—developer and public tester alike—is free to install it at their leisure. With it, comes the return of the Health app, vertical Safari tabs, and Siri AI app actions, among other new features. But for users of Apple's first foldable, the iPhone Duo, iOS 27.3 brings two rather notable changes—both of which are for the better.

With the second iOS 27.3 developer beta, Apple is introducing face unlock for the iPhone Duo. The foldable famously ships with Touch ID, the first new iPhone since the third-gen iPhone SE to do so. While that isn't a problem per se, many of us are used to unlocking our iPhones with our faces. This update just lets new Duo owners keep up with that muscle memory.

Now, take note: This isn't Face ID. No software update can introduce new hardware, so the iPhone Duo still doesn't have the camera tech required to power Apple's Face ID system. As such, the Duo's face unlock is likely not as secure as Face ID on other iPhones. Perhaps that's why your iPhone Duo will require Touch ID for Apple Pay and passwords, or after 45 minutes of inactivity. This feature seems to be one of pure convenience: If you want to be able to unlock your Duo with your face (at least, some of the time), you can.

What's more, this isn't a default setting. If you're running the beta, or if you're reading this after iOS 27.3 drops, you can find the option in Settings > Touch ID & Passcode.

Apple made a big deal about the continuity involved with opening and closing the iPhone Duo. As you do, your content moves with you seamlessly—a very Apple thing to do. That said, you might expect folding the Duo to lock it, but it doesn't. You need to hit the side button to actually put the phone to sleep.

iOS 27.3 changes that. If you so choose, you can enable a setting to lock your Duo whenever you close it. That won't work for everyone, of course—some users may still want to move between modes without worrying about locking their Duos. But for those who would rather lock their devices whenever they fold them up, the new option is under Settings > Display & Brightness.

#3427. Marvel Announces Guardians Of The Galaxy Crossover With First Official Look

The Guardians of the Galaxy are crossing over with a familiar Marvel character who had never met them. Throughout the decades, the Guardians of the Galaxy have always been a gloriously mismatched ragtag crew of cosmic outcasts from radically different backgrounds. While no longer as famous, the original 31st-century Guardians squad that brought together Vance Astro, Martinex, Yondu, Charlie-27, and Starhawk thrived on clashing alien cultures long before the modern Guardians. When Dan Abnett and Andy Lanning assembled the current incarnation in 2008, the new Guardians doubled down on the eclectic formula with half-human outlaw Star-Lord, deadly Zen-Whoberi assassin Gamora, vengeful warrior Drax, cybernetic raccoon Rocket, and gentle tree-monarch Groot.

An equally varied lineup of Earth-based and galactic icons has crossed paths with, or temporarily joined, the Guardians of the Galaxy roster over the years. Mutant favorites like Peter Quill's temporary Star-Lord replacement Kitty Pryde, Iron Man, the Thing, Captain Marvel, Angela, Ant-Man, Hercules, and Nova have each suited up as official or honorary members. Beyond their own ranks, the Guardians of the Galaxy have teamed up with Thor, Doctor Strange, Beta Ray Bill, Silver Surfer, Deadpool, the brutal Frank Castle variant known as Cosmic Ghost Rider, and most recently with Spider-Man himself.

Years after welcoming a former villain into their ranks, the Guardians of the Galaxy reunite with a different member of his species.

In Jordan Morris and Luke Ross’s The Amazing Venom #3, former Spider-Man villain Fred Myers a.k.a. Boomerang, now the red-and-blue symbiote hero Comeback, travels through deep space with his symbiote partner Passenger to reach Klyntar. Running low on fuel, Fred and Passenger make an emergency stop at Knowhere, where Fred compares the local bar to the headquarters he used to share with his fellow Spider-Man rogues, the Bar With No Name. To his understated surprise, he finds Rocket Raccoon fighting the bartender inside.

Rocket’s solo presence on Knowhere is a direct result of the Guardians of the Galaxy's disbandment after Jonathan Hickman's Imperial event and Dan Abnett’s Imperial Guardians series. While Peter Quill rules Spartax as Emperor of the Galactic Union and Gamora works to rebuild a proper Guardians roster following Maximus's coup, Rocket works largely on his own. Meanwhile, members like Groot, Drax, and Mantis are still scattered after the original team broke apart. After his team-up with Spider-Man, Rocket Raccoon is acquainted with the wall-crawler's villains, which is why he isn't shocked to see the former Boomerang on Knowhere.

The Guardians of the Galaxy share a notable if surprisingly brief history with the symbiotes, highlighted most prominently during Flash Thompson’s celebrated stint aboard the team in the mid-2010s. Appointed as Earth’s official liaison to Star-Lord’s squad in Brian Michael Bendis’s Guardians of the Galaxy run and Robbie Thompson’s Venom: Space Knight, Agent Venom traveled to Klyntar, where his symbiote was temporarily cleansed of its rage. Besides Flash’s tenure as an "Agent of the Cosmos", the Guardians also crossed paths with symbiote chaos during the Venomized event and later fought off Knull’s symbiote dragons during Al Ewing’s Guardians run in the King in Black crossover.

The Guardians of the Galaxy's roster has been in constant evolution, with some of Marvel's strongest heroes having passed through their ranks.

Still, considering how close the Guardians of the Galaxy are to the symbiotes' cosmic nature, it's odd that the Guardians haven't been far closer to symbiote lore. Klyntar is an ancient cosmic civilization tied to Celestials, Gorr the God Butcher, and the same areas of space that heroes like Star-Lord, Gamora, and Rocket patrol every day. Yet, symbiote sagas like Absolute Carnage, King in Black, and Queen in Black have largely unfolded on Earth rather than among the stars. Curiously enough, it takes characters like Fred Myers and Passenger a trip from Earth to Knowhere for a Guardian to meet another symbiote.

#3425. ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch

Even six decades into his Hollywood career, Steven Spielberg is still synonymous with a brand of movie magic and spectacle that very few can rival. And when he decides to direct a new popcorn blockbuster like “Disclosure Day,” you know you’re in for a few dazzling sequences.

One of the most exciting moments in the film comes when a train collides into a car with stars Josh O’Connor and Emily Blunt close at hand. The sequence tested every department, from camera and production design to visual effects. And during IndieWire’s recent Craft Roundtables, VFX Supervisor Matthew Butler explained the unique challenge of incorporating subtle VFX work into a scene where so much happens in camera. Related Stories If There’s Generative AI in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ It’s Not the First Time David Fincher’s Used It Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage

“With Steven, he wants everything to be as practical as it can be,” Butler said. “We had a real train. A real train, a real car attached to that train, it was being dragged on a real track. That actually did happen.”

But while Spielberg’s preferences were clear, Butler clarified that blockbusters on this scale rarely come down to a binary choice between practical effects and VFX. The biggest scenes often contain elements of both, as the pairing between in-camera human acting and cutting edge post-production is what leads to movie magic.

“When you combine some of the live action blue screen work, clearly that’s your lead actor and actress there, and your stunt work where it’s like ‘Oh my God, that looks really real’ and the stuff that you just can’t do that’s just too dangerous … that’s where visual effects came in,” he said. “But I wouldn’t say it was a visual effects sequence. It was a sequence that contained all of those, and it came together in the right way.”

More coverage from IndieWire’s Craft Roundtables will be published here over the coming weeks.

#3423. The Android camera app that doesn’t overprocess adds new color grading sets, expands to iPhone

VWFNDR + MBL, an Android camera app that doesn’t overprocess and delivers high-quality DNG (RAW) files, is getting a 2.0 release with improved color grading and an expansion to the iPhone.

VWFNDR + MBL launched on Android in May 2026 with a few points that stood out. A unique UI that adapts to the shot, minimal processing for a natural look, and support for DNG files at a level that only Google’s Pixel Camera app can truly compete with.

The app has been downloaded over 300,000 times since then, and is now getting a pretty substantial update.

On Android, this comes in the form of new color grading profiles built into the app. “NATURAL,” “NIHON,” or “B+W.” The app still saves an unprocessed DNG alongside the JPG and the grading adapts across the frame rather than having a fixed result, keeping highlights and shadows in place.

Colour grades: MBL still records unprocessed Bayer RAW DNG, and the JPG it renders alongside now uses one of three grades: NATURAL, NIHON, or B+W. Grading happens on VWFNDR’s own spatial engine. Instead of applying a fixed LUT, it adapts across the frame, much like a raw editor, so highlights and shadows keep their detail. The DNG stays untouched.

The rest of VWFNDR + MBL 2.0 takes place off of Android.

In a rare case of the tables turning, MBL was released first on Android, and only on Android for the first several months. But VWFNDR is now bringing the app to iPhone with support for variable aperture on iPhone 18 Pro and Content Credentials, Apple’s version of the C2PA standard that’s meant to prove a photo is real and not AI-generated.

#3421. Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage

Looks like Hollywood could be heading into the new year with relief on a national level. The push to pass a federal film and television tax credit by the end of 2026 picked up momentum on Friday at a White House press conference, where President Trump said his administration was actively negotiating the measure and predicted it would pass.

“It’s running its way through Congress, and it has unbelievable support,” Trump said. He singled out Senator Adam Schiff, the California Democrat who introduced the bill with Republican Senator Tim Scott of South Carolina back in September, and said, “I tell you what, Adam Schiff said, ‘Wow, we love that bill.’ Adam Schiff said that.” Related Stories Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Debuts to Mighty $120 Million, Reviving Lionsgate’s Most Important Franchise Box Office: A24’s ‘You Can See Everything’ Crosses $100 Million Globally

Trump mentioned Georgia and New Jersey by name as states with good tax credits for film and TV production, but argued that those incentives alone would not bring enough production work back from overseas. With a federal credit, he said, “Hollywood would open again.”

Trump said his administration was also negotiating whether to extend the measure to benefit movie theaters, but said the matter was unsettled. He first publicly called for a federal production incentive in August after meeting with actor Jon Voight: one of three industry “special ambassadors” he appointed early last year.

The bill’s sponsors announced more than 60 new House cosponsors and four new Senate cosponsors on Thursday morning — with lawmakers from both parties signing on in both chambers. The following day, Trump himself brought up the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act in response to a question about whether he could work with Democrats. Calling the bill “very bipartisan,” he said, “I can tell you right now it’s going to happen.”

Trump gave no timetable, though earlier this week, Representative Linda Sánchez, one of the bill’s House sponsors from California, called for Congress to pass it before 2027 so productions could qualify for benefits on the first of the year.

“Members of both parties have watched jobs in their districts move overseas,” she said in a release from Schiff’s office sent to the press. “Momentum is on our side, and we need to strike while the iron is hot by passing this bill before the end of the year.”

A floor vote has yet to be announced, but multiple sources told IndieWire the measure would move faster if attached to a stopgap government funding bill. If passed and approved, the federal initiative would give qualifying film and TV productions a 20 percent credit on labor expenses for American workers. The credit could reach 30 percent for productions that qualify for bonuses.

For crews accustomed to watching projects follow tax breaks to Canada or the U.K., the proposal would give producers a clear financial incentive to keep that work here for them in the U.S. The bill’s new Senate cosponsors include Republicans Katie Britt of Alabama and Thom Tillis of North Carolina — as well as Democrats Chris Coons of Delaware and Dick Durbin of Illinois.

The AFL-CIO and the American Hotel & Lodging Association also endorsed the bill, joining a coalition that already included IATSE, SAG-AFTRA, the Directors Guild of America, and the Motion Picture Association.

“Given the support from Republicans and Democrats in both chambers and the president, we can get this legislation across the finish line,” Schiff said.

Warning: Spoilers for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping

The Hunger Games series has never been one to shy away from putting its characters through the most unimaginable horrors. But the latest movie in the franchise, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, just might take the cake. Author Suzanne Collins took the brutality in this one to a whole new (and devastating) level, putting readers through some of the darkest moments in the franchise's history. From the Capitol's calculated cruelty to the horrifying propaganda they promote, this story is a reminder of just how little control the districts held before Katniss entered the Games.

Set during the Second Quarter Quell, the latest from the Hunger Games franchise centers around one of the most brutal Games yet, with 48 tributes fighting to the death. With twice as many children thrown into the arena, the stakes are that much higher and the losses are seemingly endless. The book itself doesn't hold back from these heart wrenching losses either, going into the nitty-gritty gory details of what really went down in the arena.

While it's totally understandable that the filmmakers need to make adjustments to the story to maintain its PG-13 rating, several of the novel's more disturbing moments unfortunately didn't make the cut. One particularly disturbing moment was missing from Sunrise on the Reaping's ending, which was the grisly death of Wellie.

One of the most horrifying moments in the Sunrise on the Reaping book is when Wellie meets her demise. While the movie doesn't nearly showcase how gruesome her death is, Suzanne Collins did not hold back. During the Games, Silka, District 1's tribute, kills Wellie by cutting off her head with an axe, making it one of the most memorable and brutal deaths the series has seen so far.

The violence isn't the only part of Wellie's death that makes this moment so painful. It also reveals how ruthless Silka has become. At this point in the Games, whatever humanity Silka had left has ultimately disappeared. And all that's left is her animalistic instinct to survive, no matter what it takes. She's no longer just a tribute determined to win, she is a savage, willing to commit unimaginable acts of violence in order to win. Her transformation is so important to the story, especially in contrast to Haymitch's much more merciful attitude.

And of course, the broadcast doesn't necessarily see this death play out the way Haymitch does in the book. Wellie's death all points back to Sunrise on the Reaping's theme of how the Capitol uses propaganda to maintain their power. This death, in particular, shows the devastating consequences on the kids' psyche while they're in the Games, and the movie's choice to leave it out is all the more disappointing.

It's not particularly surprising that Sunrise on the Reaping changed the way Wellie's death is depicted in the film. Despite the already dark subject matter of the series, the films have kept a PG-13 rating, meaning that filmmakers have had to be strategic about how much graphic violence they can actually show.

These movies certainly aren't lacking in death or violence, but they often rely on quick cuts and character reactions instead of showing every brutal detail. In an interview with Entertainment Weekly, SOTR director Francis Lawrence explained:

“What’s great about Suzanne’s writing is that she pulls no punches. The only thing we have to do in the movies is make them PG-13. So there's certain things she describes in the book that I could never put in the movies. There’s a character holding the head of a child at one point in the book, and that’s just not something you can do in a PG-13 movie.”

Wellie's death presents a very difficult challenge because her decapitation is much more graphic than a PG-13 audience would expect to see. Showing that death the way it's written in the book would have pushed the movie into a more restrictive place, with the risk of losing a huge part of its audience. As a result, Silka still murdered Wellie, but it is significantly less graphic.

While it's understandable that Sunrise on the Reaping couldn't recreate every gruesome detail of Wellie's death without potentially jeopardizing its PG-13 rating, that doesn't mean the filmmakers made the right decision by toning down the moment. In fact, leaving out the nature of her death takes away from one of the most disturbing turning points in the story.

Wellie's decapitation isn't just part of the story for shock value, but it's an important indicator of how high the Second Quarter Quell's stakes have become. It shows how far tributes are willing to go to survive.

More importantly, the moment says a lot about Silka and the role she has in the Sunrise on the Reaping cast. Wellie was one of the younger tributes and not particularly dangerous, so Silka didn't necessarily need to decapitate her. Wellie was never a true threat to Silka, or anybody, for that matter. But in losing this moment in the film, her transition into true savagery isn't shown.

Now, the filmmakers didn't necessarily need to show the death in every graphic detail to preserve the meaning of the scene. A longer sequence, stronger reactions from Haymitch and Silka, or more attention to the aftermath could have communicated the same horror without pushing the movie past its PG-13 rating.

Beyond changing the circumstances of Wellie's death, Sunrise on the Reaping missed the opportunity to do more with her as a character. With 48 tributes, it naturally has a lot of characters to introduce with stories to balance, but that shouldn't mean the minor characters have to fade into the background.

In the Sunrise on the Reaping novel, Wellie is a District 6 tribute and a member of Haymitch and Ampert's alliance, The Newcomers. She is also one of the kids in the arena who quickly realizes everything is poisonous. On the last day of the Games, Haymitch sticks with Wellie and hides her under a tree while he goes to locate dry kindling. In his mind, Wellie was to be the victor, and he was going to try his hardest to make that happen.

This is what makes her death even more heartbreaking. Haymitch saw Wellie as worth protecting because he thought she'd be a much better victor than himself. His choice to stay with her also shows that he genuinely believed she'd have a chance of making it out alive.

In the movie, Wellie is only seen for a couple of seconds when Haymitch offers her his lunch. Had that connection been established earlier, viewers would have had more of a reason to care about her before she died. Her relationship with Haymitch could've reinforced his arc in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping even more.

#3418. Before ‘Ted Lasso,’ HBO’s Forgotten 5-Part Sports Series Was Perfect From Start to Finish

When people talk about Dwayne "The Rock" Johnson today, the spotlight is usually on his blockbuster career. Since his film debut in The Mummy Returns back in 2001, he’s become one of the most bankable stars in Hollywood, anchoring franchises like Fast & Furious and Jumanji, voicing Disney favorites as he does in Moana, and exploring dramatic work in The Smashing Machine. But while he was dominating the box office, Johnson also made a detour into television that gave him room to show a different side of himself.

That detour was HBO's Ballers, which premiered in 2015 and ran for five seasons. Following Johnson as a retired football player turned financial manager, the series was a quiet game-changer. It proved he could carry a character-driven drama, dig into complex storylines, and show range far beyond action and comedy. While Ballers never reached the cultural relevance of Succession or Game of Thrones, it carved out a loyal fanbase and gave Johnson the opportunity to show his talent ranged much further than charisma and muscles.

Ballers is sort of like Entourage in the world of sports, but Johnson’s Spencer Strasmore is far more layered than that shorthand suggests. A former NFL star forced into retirement by injuries, Spencer reinvented himself as a financial manager for current players. That setup opened the door to endless drama, comedy, and scandal as he tried to guide his clients through the pitfalls of fame, wealth, and the bad decisions that often came with both.

At its best, Ballers used the world of sports to explore bigger issues. It spotlighted the dangers of concussions and player safety, the financial risks of sudden wealth, and the sacrifices athletes make to keep playing the game they love. While the show had plenty of Miami flash and glamour, it never shied away from the painful reality of what happens when the spotlight fades. Spencer’s own demons, haunted by concussions and desperate to stay relevant, grounded the story and gave Johnson one of his most complex roles on screen.

For audiences who only knew him as “The Rock” or as the face of blockbuster tentpoles, his role in Ballers was a revelation. Johnson brought surprising vulnerability beneath the swagger, delivering a performance that balanced confidence with self-doubt. And yes, he looked great in those suits, but it wasn’t just another cool-guy role for the bona fide movie star. It was proof he could anchor a drama with real emotional depth.

When Ballers premiered, Johnson was already a global star, but his filmography leaned heavily on action tentpoles and family comedies. He was bankable, but not necessarily considered versatile. Playing Spencer across five seasons gave him the chance to shift that perception, proving he could handle long-form storytelling and layered character work that his usual projects didn’t always allow. Johnson wasn't just coasting on his charm, playing a character who was constantly at war with himself. On one hand, he'd negotiate million-dollar deals, while dealing with his private struggle with painkillers and the concussions he'd endured as a player.

Johnson shined in Spencer's most vulnerable moments when that mask slipped, showing a man who didn't want to admit he wasn't physically or mentally okay. It's a departure from his more "tough guy" roles, giving his familiar swagger a brittle edge. He wanted more than anything to prove he still belonged in the room, but carrying the weight of not being able to play anymore was a difficult burden for him to carry at times, and Johnson portrayed that struggle with an authenticity that was truly the heartbeat of the show.

The role also carried personal meaning for Johnson. When he announced the show’s cancellation on social media, he reflected on never getting the chance to play in the NFL as he once dreamed, but that Ballers gave him “the opportunity to play a character that loved the game.” That sincerity came through on-screen, especially in scenes where Spencer tried to mentor some of those players like Ricky (John David Washington), warning him not to repeat his mistakes, or when he pushed Charles (Omar Miller) to find pride in life after football. And even in his lighter moments with his boss, played by the hilarious Rob Corddry, Johnson proved he could be the center of a strong ensemble cast week to week. Add in cameos from real athletes like NBA star Steph Curry and NFL Super Bowl Champion Odell Beckham Jr., and Ballers felt authentic while still entertaining.

Behind the camera, the show solidified Johnson’s multi-hyphenate status. Serving as an executive producer alongside Mark Wahlberg, he proved he could shepherd a project as well as headline it, which is a skill set that paved the way for his current role shaping entire franchises. The show’s reach even extended into politics, with Massachusetts Senator Elizabeth Warren famously naming it her favorite series during her 2019 presidential campaign because of the way it spotlighted real-world issues facing athletes. It was proof not only of Johnson’s broad appeal, but also of the show’s surprisingly sharp storytelling.

Looking back, Ballers should have been much bigger, especially given Johnson’s popularity at the time, but for whatever reason, it flew a little under the radar. Today, it’s often remembered as one of HBO’s most underrated gems, and in a world with sports dramas like Friday Night Lights and Ted Lasso, it deserves to be mentioned among the best of the genre. More importantly, it became the perfect vehicle for Dwayne Johnson to prove he was more than just a global movie star and gave him the chance to stretch as an actor, grow as a producer, and show audiences a side of himself they hadn’t seen before.

And in many ways, it laid the groundwork for roles like The Smashing Machine, but its five-season run is worth revisiting on its own terms. The deals and scandals keep things moving, while Spencer’s struggles give you a reason to keep watching.

#3417. If There’s Generative AI in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ It’s Not the First Time David Fincher’s Used It

The uproar over the alleged use of generative AI imagery in “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” has taken a familiar path. Early responses to the Netflix film penned by Quentin Tarantino and directed by David Fincher have pointed out egregious examples of generative video artifacts sticking out in key flashback moments in the film — including one shot from the trailer where it certainly looks like a video AI program rendered a wagon the wrong way around.

The criticism is of the use of generative AI in principle as a fundamental betrayal of the creative process — but it’s also of Fincher, as a director who, historically, has been meticulous with the level of detail and intention in every single shot of his films. In the early responses to Fincher’s latest, there’s been a lot of surprise and disappointment about this particular filmmaker being caught up in an AI controversy. Related Stories Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Debuts to Mighty $120 Million, Reviving Lionsgate’s Most Important Franchise Box Office: A24’s ‘You Can See Everything’ Crosses $100 Million Globally

At first blush, his approach seems at odds with using generative AI video, which relies on regurgitated (and, it bears repeating every time, stolen) data. But Fincher has defended his use of AI to the LA Times as a way to continue to innovate on an art form that is, after all, just over a hundred years old.

That defense really shouldn’t be surprising, given Fincher’s history with AI specifically. Although he’s been critical of generative tools in the past, Fincher admitted to using them (never publicly disclosing which) in the 4K remaster of “Se7en,” which the director described as a process of needing to remake the negative in order to battle the ravages of time (and the thousands of tiny scratches that would show up in 4K). “If you could see a 30-year-old negative and what it looks like even when immaculately stored — it was an enormous amount of fixing, just digs and scratches and cinch,” he told EW at the time.

That kind of image restoration technology was around long, long before the Anthropic IPO failed to save the stock market, but its level of precision has increased enormously in the past year. There were also sequences in the stored “Se7en,” though, where generative tech filled in gaps from the original. For one example, Fincher talked about a moment where a camera pan overshot the mark and changedh a shot. The performance had been good enough to use a technically flawed take — and, combined wit an unused take, allowed software to generate the missing information and restore the intended image.

“It ends up being the most thrillingly stupid fix in the world because if you see it, we didn’t do our jobs. And you probably won’t see it. You probably won’t be aware that it’s happened. But you look at it, and you just think to yourself, ‘It’s so nice that we can fix that kind of stuff today,'” Fincher told Collider about that moment in “Se7en.”

By Fincher’s own lights, then, the problem with AI in “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is that people are painfully aware of it. AI critics might make a distinction between video restoration tools that work on existing projects and those tools being used because they can more quickly and cheaply generate originals that would’ve otherwise needed to be crafted by human hands. Having something AI-generated isn’t necessarily better than nothing when it comes to art, and choosing to AI-generate a Western chase sequence inside of, say, 10 seconds isn’t a solution to all.

Still, Fincher knows what he’s doing. This past week, he emphasized to the LA Times that he’s not a Luddite when it comes to film: “We’re talking about a thing that’s a hundred years old, and everyone’s going, ‘Stop. Pencils down. No more iterating. It’s not necessary to have at your fingertips the ability to change the color of that person’s eyes.’ Well, it exists. Should we not use it?”

The answer is an emphatic “No!” to some And they can certainly be mad, or disappointed, or disheartened about Fincher’s decision to use AI tools. The one thing they shouldn’t be is surprised.

#3414. Box Office: A24’s ‘You Can See Everything’ Crosses $100 Million Globally

“You Can See Everything,” an unconventional documentary about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes in exile, has crossed $100 million at the global box office. Its success extends a hot streak for A24, the indie studio behind last summer’s blockbuster “Backrooms” as well as arthouse hits such as “The Drama” and “Primetime.”

“You Can See Everything” now ranks as the eighth-highest grossing non-music documentary, moving ahead of “Deep Sea 3D,” and the second-highest grossing non-music and non-nature documentary, behind Michael Moore’s “Fahrenheit 9/11.” It’s unlikely to surpass Moore’s anti-Bush jeremiad, which grossed an astonishing $222.4 million when it opened in the height of a fiercely contested presidential election. Related Stories If There’s Generative AI in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ It’s Not the First Time David Fincher’s Used It Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage

Those aren’t the only benchmarks with which to measure “You Can See Everything’s” impact. It is now the seventh-highest grossing film in the history of A24, coming in behind “Materialists,” which earned $105.6 million globally. On a domestic basis, “You Can See Everything” is A24’s third-highest grossing film, ranking just behind “Backrooms” ($197.5 million) and “Marty Supreme” ($96 million). It should easily surpass “Marty Supreme” and that film had Timothée Chalamet and a boatload of Oscar noms behind it.

“You Can See Everything,” which is co-directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, earned $2.5 million this weekend to bring its domestic haul to $93.5 million after six weeks of release. Most of its earnings have been stateside. It’s currently playing in Australia, the U.K., and Scandinavia and the studio said its international rollout will continue over the next several weeks.

A24 is trying to keep the hits coming with “Club Kid.” Jordan Firstman’s look at a party promoter forced to grow up when he discovers he has a son, grossed $1.4 million on 229 screens in limited release this weekend. It has earned $3.4 million since it debuted three weeks ago. A24 bought the film out of Cannes for $17 million.

#3413. 10 Books Like ‘Dungeon Crawler Carl’ You Should Read Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

There’s nothing quite like Dungeon Crawler Carl, Matt Dinniman’s hilarious, inventive, and surprisingly emotional book series about a man in his underwear forced to fight his way through a livestreamed game show based on dungeon-crawling video games that takes place after an alien takeover of Earth. (Did I mention he's accompanied by his ex-girlfriend’s suddenly talkative cat?)

The premise should not work, but it sure does—and it makes more sense if you know it fits into a popular genre known as "LitRPG," a blend of "literature" and "role-playing game." If you've torn through all eight books released so far and you're looking for more reads that blend surprisingly deep hilarity with tabletop and video game rules (or just similar feels), here are 10 books you should check out.

An isekai story that lands in the sweet spot for DCC fans, He Who Fights with Monsters kicks off with Jason—a completely normal, kind of boring middle manager—waking up in a strange hedge maze, completely nude (even his hair is gone). He has magic that works like a video game, and has to deal with quests that slowly give him clothes (it’s a relief when he finally acquires some pants), force him to survive cannibals, and hunt down various monsters that definitely need killing. It’s got the same “gaming rules” structure as DCC and a similarly absurdist tone, with just the right spice of darkness.

The Cradle series by Will Wight isn’t a LitRPG, and it doesn’t have Carl’s focus on humor, but it’s another progression fantasy with enough game-like elements to be a great match. Lindon is an “unsouled,” incapable of gaining any of the sacred arts and doomed to a life without a future. His lack of power makes Lindon ferociously determined to find an alternative path to power and success, and that’s what drives this story. He has to find creative ways to move forward, and slowly this leads him to a path that just might make him the most powerful person in his world. DCC fans will love the progression and the tone.

One of the key elements of any video game is the respawn—you get killed, but you pop back up to try again, sometimes at the beginning, sometimes at a save point. Django Wexler leverages that mechanic to great effect in How to Become the Dark Lord and Die Trying. Davi has been summoned to a fantasy world to be the hero, the person who defeats the Dark Lord and saves the day—but she’s failed (and died) so many times, she’s fed up, and decides that on this run through, she’s going to switch sides and become the Dark Lord, using all her knowledge gained from endless replays to her advantage. The humor is pitch-black the way DCC fans like it, and the progressive structure is a perfect fit.

Is Princess Donut your favorite part of Dungeon Crawler Carl? Of course she is. In that case, check out Andrew Seiple’s Threadbare series. Threadbare is a stuffed bear brought to magical life in a failed experiment. He’s a foot tall, full of stuffing, and extremely dumb when the story begins. But when he’s rescued by a little girl and plunged into a horrible series of dangers, Threadbare has to find a way to level up. Like DCC, Threadbare starts off leaning into the absurdity and humor, then slowly gains emotional gravitas as the story progresses.

If you play tabletop RPGs, you’ve encountered a Murderhobo or two: A character who solves all their problems by killing—even members of their own party. Luke doesn’t aspire to be a Murderhobo—he just wants to take over the family business and hang with his buddies. But when an invasion threatens the kingdom, everyone over the age of 17 is ordered to be tested for Potential. Luke’s friends all test high and join the Ascender Corps, traveling to different planes for training. Luke tests ... very low, and when he steps through a portal to engage in his training, he finds himself without any guidance or training in a strange, deadly world where his only chance of survival is to murder his way through it. It’s dark, darkly funny, and a progression fantasy like no other.

If you’re looking for a book series that combines the dark, chaotic humor, absurd game mechanics, and surprising emotional depth of Carl, here’s Ryan “Quicksave” Romano, a man who has the unique ability to literally create a save point in his existence that allows him to go back and redo things whenever he dies. Searching for a childhood friend, he becomes embroiled in a violent gang war that lets him make good use of his power—but underneath the snark and the insanity of Ryan’s existence is a surprisingly affecting story of a man who has suffered, and suffered countless tragedies that are definitely taking their toll.

If your fave bit of DCC is Carl himself—a mediocre dude in an extraordinary situation—you should read Dennis E. Taylor’s fantastic Bobiverse books. Bob is a software engineer who hits it big and promptly dies, waking up to discover a century has passed and he’s been repurposed as an AI controlling a space probe searching for new planets for humanity to inhabit. If he fails in his mission (and he’s not the only probe out there), he’ll be turned off for good. Luckily, he can make copies of himself, and he’s pretty smart. The humor here is smart and soaked in pop culture, making it a perfect match for DCC fans.

Want more of Carl’s absurdist humor? Mayor of Noobtown is the LitRPG you’re looking for. Jim dies and wakes up in a video game-esque universe and finds himself stuck in the zone designated for newbies—players with no experience, skill, or hope. The area fell out of the mainline progression mechanic a long time ago, so there doesn’t seem to be a way to gain power, and the monsters are not at all concerned about the unfairness of it all, so Jim has to figure out how to advance in a universe that seems designed to kill him (again).

If you want to lean into the meta side of things, check out Scathing Reviewer, written by an author who goes by the unusual pen name "BananaDragon." Liu Peijin is the author of a sprawling LitRPG web novel, and she’s used to the bad reviews and complaints from readers—and quite combative about it. When her books’ universe blossoms into a very dangerous new reality, she should be perfectly positioned to survive, having written the story in the first place. But her story becoming real also means her insufferable protagonist is real, and all those nasty critics are now passing judgment on her entire existence. It’s a dark, funny takedown of the entire genre itself, and DCC fans will love it.

If you want a story that parallels the dungeon crawling aspect of DCC, Andrew Rowe’s Arcane Ascension series is the ticket. The Serpent Spire is a tower of constantly changing traps, puzzles, and dangerous creatures. If you enter and survive, you emerge with magical powers. Corin Cadence’s brother entered the Serpent Spire years ago and never returned—and now Corin is determined not only to survive, but to make it to the top, where legend says a goddess will grant you whatever you wish. And what Corin wants is his brother back. It’s a literal progression combined with LitRPG rules, game-inspired puzzle-solving, and a complex magic system that fans of Carl will definitely enjoy.

#3412. Wizard Of Oz Gets A Mad Max Twist In Dark New Adaptation Releasing In 3 Months

David Pepose’s comic book The O.Z. has found a home with Boom! Studios, and he explains what the series is about and how the idea came to be.

David Pepose is one of the most versatile writers in comics. Readers can see him bringing Layla El-Faouly from the MCU's Moon Knight to Marvel Comics and writing the amazing Cable: Love and Chrome. Then, he’ll turn around and give horror fans an amazing comic book like Mad Cave Studios' The Devil That Wears My Face. Among the amazing comics David Pepose has written is a bold reimagining of the classic book and movie, The Wizard of Oz, The O.Z.

The O.Z. began its push on Kickstarter, but was recently picked up by Boom! Studios. In a recent interview ScreenRant was fortunate enough to have with Pepose, he talks about what the story is about, the way it came to be, and more.

The O.Z. is one of the most creative changes to the classic book and movie. When asked about what the story is about, Pepose goes into great detail about it and why it's different from other Wizard of Oz tales.

David Pepose: THE O.Z. is like Mad Max meets The Wizard of Oz — it’s the story of Dorothy Gale’s granddaughter and namesake, who is an Iraq war veteran grappling with PTSD and disillusionment. But when our new Dorothy is caught up in a tornado, she finds herself stranded in the land of Oz — where she learns her grandmother’s adventures plunged the country into a brutal civil war. Now Dorothy must team up with the Tin Soldier, the Prince of Lions, and Jack Pumpkinhead in order to find the Silver Slippers and bring peace to the Occupied Zone… or as the locals call it, The O.Z.

Many people have brought different versions of The Wizard of Oz to various genres, but Pepose's has been the most adventurous. Considering the source material, that says a lot. When asked about that, he said, "I’ve always been a fan of mashing up different genres, so doing a fantasy war story was something I’d wanted to do early in my career." However, how he landed on The Wizard of Oz is a funny story.

Pepose: Landing on The Wizard of Oz came across as kind of a happy accident — I was typing different fantasy staples to see if anything could serve as inspiration, and my cursor froze in the middle of the word “Oz.” That had me thinking about the word Oz as an acronym, which turned into “Occupied Zone” — and that moment instantly crystallized the entire narrative for me.

When asked why he went this particular route with Dorothy, Pepose gives an interesting reason.

Pepose: Back in my days as a newspaper reporter, I’d interviewed a ton of returning veterans about their experiences coming back home, and those stories had always stuck with me — and that became the basis for Dorothy’s story in THE O.Z.

Now that The O.Z. has been picked up by Boom! Studios, the next question is whether or not the series will continue. Pepose seems hopeful that this won’t be the last comic book fans will see of the characters and this alternate reality Wizard of Oz story. However, there are some factors to consider.

Pepose: Never say never! Whether we do a sequel storyline will ultimately be determined by demand and me and Ruben Rojas’ respective schedules, but I do have a few ideas in my back pocket, which I’d actually pitched to BOOM!’s Editor-in-Chief Andy Schmidt and our O.Z. editor Gregory Hopkins. So there’s definitely room to return to the Occupied Zone if enough people demand it.

The O.Z. #1 is scheduled to be released in February 2027 by Boom! Studios.

#3411. iPhone 18, iPhone Air 2 get new release timing updates

Apple only launched high-end ‘Pro’ and ‘Duo’ iPhones this fall, marking a departure from previous years when more affordable models debuted too. But iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 are still coming, and a new report offers an update on release timing.

A new report from Kim Yeong-ho at ETNews provides a fresh update on timing for the iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2.

Rumors have indicated for well over a year that Apple planned to push these models out of the typical fall launch window and introduce them in early 2027 instead.

Per ETNews, Samsung and LG are providing the display panels for the new models, with Samsung the sole supplier for iPhone Air 2 and both companies splitting orders for iPhone 18. And their mass production plans signal a March release for the products.

Samsung Display plans to begin mass production in January, while LG Display will start late this year…The Korean panel makers appear to be aligning their production plans with an expected March launch.

A March launch window lines up well with when Apple tends to ramp up product introductions following a slower winter. Earlier this year, iPhone 17e debuted in March alongside new Macs and the iPad Air.

The year before, however, the iPhone 16e arrived in February instead.

With Apple shaking up its normal iPhone rollout schedule, it was anyone’s guess how soon the new models would debut. But a March launch makes sense and gives Apple a trio of new iPhones every six months—three unveiled in September, and another three in March.

#3410. ‘Sunrise on the Reaping’ Officially Rebels Against Critics With Massive Audience Score

Erielle Sudario is a Collider News and Feature Author from Australia and has worked in the journalism industry since 2018. She has a passion for entertainment and pop culture news and has interviewed YouTubers, voice actors, film directors, and musicians throughout her career. When she's not writing, you can see Erielle building keyboards, reading a good book, playing video games, and creating content on social media.

The latest installment of The Hunger Games has arrived, and audiences have spoken. The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is the second prequel in Suzanne Collins' popular YA dystopian franchise, and it didn't sit well with critics upon release. But what about audiences? Now that the movie has entered theaters, the viewers have spoken about their return to Panem.

Sunrise on the Reaping takes place 24 years before the events of the first Hunger Games story, during the 2nd Quarter Quell, a special Hunger Games with new rules added every 25 years to remind the districts of their defeat in the rebellion. This is the game Haymitch Abernathy participated in, now played by Joseph Zada, and the new rules for this Hunger Games were that each district would send double the number of tributes, increasing the total from 24 to 48 children in the arena.

When the critics' score came out, Sunrise on the Reaping debuted with a 74% rating on Rotten Tomatoes, and as of writing, the number has dropped to 67%. However, now that the movie has entered theaters, audiences disagree, and it sits at a 95% Verified Hot Audience Score. Audience reception was also positive on Letterboxd, with the film earning a 4.1-star rating. Collider's Victoria Luxford gave Sunrise on the Reaping an 8/10 score in her review. She praised the movie's "dark and gritty" portrayal of Collins' world but criticized the runtime, especially for those "not heavily invested" in the series.

Ever since The Hunger Games film franchise began in 2012, six films have been released: four main movies and two prequels. According to Rotten Tomatoes critics' scores, the highest-rated Hunger Games movie is the sequel, The Hunger Games: Catching Fire, with a 90% score, followed by the first Hunger Games movie at 85%. And despite Sunrise on the Reaping's low critics' score, the lowest-rated Hunger Games movie from critics is the first prequel film, The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, with a 64% rating.

Audiences, however, viewed the franchise differently: Sunrise on the Reaping is the audience's highest-rated Hunger Games movie ever, followed by Catching Fire with an 89% rating, then the first Hunger Games movie with an 81% audience score. The audience's lowest-rated installment is The Hunger Games: Mockingjay, Part 2, with an audience score of 66% on Rotten Tomatoes.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is now showing in theaters. Follow Collider for more updates.

Taking place in Panem 24 years prior to the original series, this new Hunger Games entry focuses on the reaping of the 50th Hunger Games.

#3408. Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Debuts to Mighty $120 Million, Reviving Lionsgate’s Most Important Franchise

“The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” made quick work of the competition, debuting to an impressive $120 million and easily capturing the top spot on the domestic box office chart.

The sequel represents a massive improvement on the opening of its predecessor, 2023’s “The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes,” which bowed with $44 million, a franchise low. However, “Sunrise on the Reaping” didn’t match the highs of the series. Its opening pales in comparison to 2013’s “Catching Fire” ($158 million debut), 2012’s OG “Hunger Games” ($152.5 million), and 2014’s “Mockingjay Part 1” ($121.8 million debut). Deadline trumpeted the fact that the film has the second highest-grossing opening for a prequel behind “Rogue One,” which seems like a milestone no one really ever thought or cared about before. So extra credit to some enterprising studio publicist or Google for unearthing that gem. Related Stories Box Office: A24’s ‘You Can See Everything’ Crosses $100 Million Globally If There’s Generative AI in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ It’s Not the First Time David Fincher’s Used It

But whatever records it holds, “Sunrise on the Reaping” has revived a series that was looking a little long in the tooth. Why did this “Hunger Games” outpace “The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes”? It probably helped that franchise icons Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson, and Woody Harrelson were coaxed back for brief appearances. There was also a top-shelf cast that included Oscar winner Kieran Culkin, Oscar nominees Glenn Close, Elle Fanning, Ralph Fiennes, and Jesse Plemons, and rising stars like Iris Apatow, Mckenna Grace, Ben Wang, and Joseph Zada. Internationally, “Sunrise on the Reaping” earned $105 million from 84 territories, pushing its worldwide box office gross to $225 million.

Lionsgate is distributing the $150 million production, as it has the previous films. The studio recently mounted something of a comeback under Adam Fogelson, who replaced Joe Drake as the motion picture chief in 2024. Lionsgate was on its back foot at the time, having released flops like “Borderlands” and the reboot of “The Crow.” In recent months, its fortunes have shifted thanks to blockbusters like “Michael” and hits such as “The Housemaid” and “The Long Walk.” A revived “Hunger Games” franchise is critical, as it gives Lionsgate another pillar for its slate.

But “The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes” success threatened to overshadow “I Play Rocky.” The Amazon MGM Studios release earned $9.3 million after expanding from 29 locations to 2,477 theaters. It’s playing like gangbusters, earning an A+ CinemaScore, a rare distinction that puts it in the company of “Top Gun: Maverick” and “The Avengers.” The word-of-mouth is clearly excellent, which could help it build momentum over the holidays. It’s also worth noting that “I Play Rocky” is catering to older moviegoers who take their time getting around to seeing things. Even if it starts to fade, “I Play Rocky” is a relatively economical bet. It cost in the $30 million range to produce and has earned $10.4 million since it debuted.

Then there’s “Ebenezer.” The Johnny Depp revival isn’t as glorious as his most diehard fans may have hoped. The Christmas story fell roughly 60 percent in its second weekend, earning $7.7 million to bring its domestic total to $32.5 million. But Paramount didn’t spend lavishly to make the film. It only cost $38 million to remind Depp’s Scrooge of the Christmas spirit. “Ebenezer” has also earned $45.9 million internationally, bringing its global total to a respectable $78.4 million.

Among the newcomers, Sumerian Pictures released “Josephine,” a family drama with Gemma Chan and Channing Tatum,” on four screens in New York and Los Angeles this weekend, grossing an estimated $84,200 for a per-screen average of $21,050. The film earned raves at Sundance where it premiered and Sumerian bought it. “Elsinore,” a drama about Ian Charleson’s final stage performance, opened with $240,000 from six locations in New York and Los Angeles for a per-theater average of $40,000. Focus Features is distributing the film, which has earned Oscar buzz for Andrew Scott. Lastly, Janus Films and Criterion debuted Paul Thomas Anderson’s concert film “Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall” in three locations, where it earned $162,000 for $54,000 per-screen average. The film is only showing in 35mm, which limits the number of screenings available to cinephiles and PTA completists.

#3407. iPhone Duo is getting three new features in iOS 27.3

iOS 27.3 launches next month and includes several exciting changes for iPhone Duo, here’s what’s new for Apple’s foldable model.

Apple is granting iPhone Duo users one of their biggest feature requests: face unlock is coming with iOS 27.3.

Face unlock isn’t a full-fledged Face ID, and it doesn’t work for features like Apple Pay, but it is a convenient new option for unlocking your iPhone Duo just by looking at it. Per Apple:

Use the front camera, along with a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication, to quickly unlock iPhone Duo when it’s closed. Face recognition data never leaves your device.

If your iPhone Duo has gone unused for 45 minutes or more, face unlock won’t work and you’ll need to authenticate with Touch ID or your passcode. But for most users, that probably just means using Touch ID first thing in the morning, then relying on face unlock the rest of the day.

On a related note, you can also enable Attention Aware features in iOS 27.3. These are available whether you use the face unlock feature or not, but are limited to the outer display. Once enabled, they can automatically lower the volume of alarms and timers, keep the display from dimming, and more.

Read more: iOS 27.3 adds new face unlock feature for iPhone Duo

Reachability is available on other iPhone models to move onscreen content down vertically, closer to your thumb. But on iPhone Duo with iOS 27.3, Apple has a unique twist on the feature.

Instead of helping you reach content vertically, Reachability on iPhone Duo works horizontally.

If you’re using the outer screen and find that buttons or other UI elements are out of reach, you can swipe from the side to have onscreen content shift closer to your thumb.

You can always disable Reachability if you find yourself accidentally triggering it too often. But if one-handed iPhone Duo use gives you trouble, Reachability is a great new option to have.

Read more: iOS 27.3 introduces new iPhone Duo feature for one-handed use

What should happen when you close your iPhone Duo’s folding screen? Apple has found that users have different preferences. Some want the iPhone to stay unlocked for continued use, while others prefer that it automatically locks when closed.

In iOS 27.3, Apple adds a new setting so users can enable whichever behavior they prefer.

By default, iPhone Duo will work as it always has, staying unlocked after being closed. But inside Settings ⇾ Display & Brightness, iOS 27.3 provides the option of automatically locking upon being closed instead. You could achieve something similar before with Shortcuts, but now there’s a built-in setting too.

It’s not exactly a “new feature,” but iPhone Duo users will also find that the system keyboard has changed in iOS 27.3. Apple tweaked the outer display keyboard to push keys closer together and make one-handed use easier.

Here’s a comparison of the old and new keyboards via Beta Profiles on X:

iOS 27.3 beta tweaks iPhone Duo's outer display keyboard, with narrower keys and a slightly thinner, smaller font. pic.twitter.com/BDKCBZc52Z

Read more: iOS 27.3 changes the iPhone Duo keyboard, here’s how

Which new iPhone Duo features in iOS 27.3 are you most excited for? Let us know in the comments.
